The **University of Illinois Chicago School of Law** (**UIC Law**) is the [law school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_school "Law school") of the [University of Illinois Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago"), a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois. Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the **John Marshall Law School** and initially accredited by the [American Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") in 1951. It merged with the [University of Illinois at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago "University of Illinois at Chicago") in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-4) On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-5) The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6) uncovered by historian [Paul Finkelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Finkelman "Paul Finkelman"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-7) had revealed that influential 19th century [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") chief justice [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall "John Marshall") was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6)

UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as [The Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). It is across the street from the [Dirksen Federal Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirksen_Federal_Building "Dirksen Federal Building"), which houses the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit "U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit") and the [U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Illinois "U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois"), and about four blocks from the [Daley Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daley_Center "Daley Center"), which houses the [Circuit Court of Cook County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_Court_of_Cook_County "Circuit Court of Cook County") and the Bilandic Building site of the [Illinois Appellate Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Appellate_Court "Illinois Appellate Court") (First District). The [Chicago Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bar_Association "Chicago Bar Association") is next door to the law school.

## Admissions and costs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Admissions and costs")]

For the class entering in 2023, UIC Law accepted 69.53% of applicants, with 27.96% of those accepted enrolling. The average enrollee had a 152 [LSAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_School_Admissions_Test "Law School Admissions Test") score and 3.39 undergraduate [GPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grading_in_education#United_States "Grading in education").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-Standard_509-1) Tuition and fees at UIC Law for the 2020-2021 academic year is $39,014 for Illinois residents and $48,014 for out of state residents.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-8)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academics")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/John_Marshall_Law.jpg/250px-John_Marshall_Law.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Marshall_Law.jpg)

The former name, John Marshall Law School

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

UIC Law has day and evening divisions, with identical instruction, course content, and scholastic requirements. Lawyering Skills courses, which focus on writing, research, and oral argument, are an integral part of the core curriculum. These courses are taught in small groups, to maximize the individual attention given to each student. A student may earn a J.D. certificate in a certain area of the law or focus more emphatically and earn a joint degree (J.D./LL.M.).

The law school also offers Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Jurisprudence (M.J.) programs for practicing attorneys and non-attorney professionals and other individual students.

UIC School of Law offers seven [Master of Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Laws "Master of Laws") (LL.M.) programs for attorneys seeking specialized education in legal issues and for current J.D. students who would like the maximum concentration in particular areas of the law. UIC Law offers a comprehensive curriculum in the following areas: Employee Benefits Law, Estate Planning, Information Technology and [Privacy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_Law "Privacy Law"), Intellectual Property Law, International Business and Trade Law, [Real Estate Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate"), and Tax Law.

### Journals and organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Journals and organizations")]

There are four honors programs: _UIC Law Review_, _[UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC\_Review\_of\_Intellectual\_Property\_Law "UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law")_ ("RIPL"), the [Moot Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moot_court "Moot court") Honors Program, and the Trial Advocacy & Dispute Resolution Honors Program.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-9) UIC Law sends teams to more than 30 moot court and mock trial competitions annually.

The student community at UIC Law includes more than 50 [student organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_society "Student society") engaging in social awareness, community service, legal discussions, and social activities.

### Clinics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Clinics")]

UIC Law students are required to earn three experiential learning credits – working in a clinic, externship, or a combination of both – in order to graduate. The law school offers students practical opportunities through its seven Community Legal Clinics and more than 50 externship placement sites. Clinics include the Community Enterprise & Solidarity Economy Clinic, Fair Housing Legal Support Center & Clinic, International Human Rights Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Patent Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Trademark Clinic, Pro Bono Litigation Clinic, and the Veterans Legal Clinic. Externship opportunities include judicial, governmental, and non-profit placements, as well as a Semester-in-Practice program that allows JD students to earn a semester of credit hours immersed in a legal market outside of Chicago.

### Global Legal Skills Conference Series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Global Legal Skills Conference Series")]

The [Global Legal Skills Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Legal_Skills_Conference "Global Legal Skills Conference") Series was founded in 2005 as a forum for professors who teach Legal English and international legal skills to exchange information on teaching techniques and materials.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-10) The conference connects legal writing professionals and other professors who have an interest in teaching international students and lawyers who speak English as a second language.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-11) Since its inception, the Global Legal Skills Conference has been held four times in Chicago, once in Washington, D.C., twice in Mexico, twice in Costa Rica, and twice in Italy.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-12) The conference now also includes presentations of GLS Awards for individual achievement, institutional vision, and outstanding publications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-14)

## Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Library")]

The Louis L. Biro Law Library occupies the 6th – 10th floors of the law school's State Street building. A team of professional librarians and staff members work to serve the students during the 96 hours/week that the library is open. The library holds over 263,003 volumes and microform equivalents and provides on-campus and remote access to some of those titles via their specialty electronic databases. It is continually adding more online subscriptions to its growing collection of electronic resources, including Lexis, Westlaw, [CALI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Computer-Assisted_Legal_Instruction "Center for Computer-Assisted Legal Instruction") Lessons, BNA Premier, IICLE SmartBooks, Max Planck Encyclopedia of Public International Law Online, Justis International Law Reports, Courtroom View Network, which contains audio versions of law school casebooks and streaming trial videos, and Mango languages, an easy to follow system for learning over 20 different languages.

Students have wireless access throughout the law school and the library offers seating for 750, including twelve group study rooms. In addition to supporting the research & instructional needs of the students, faculty & staff of the law school, the library is also open to law school alumni and members of the Chicago Bar Association, whose headquarters building is next door.

## Bar examination passage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bar examination passage")]

In 2023, the overall bar examination passage rate for the law school's first-time examination takers was 59.19%. The average first-time pass rate for [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") accredited schools was 78.14%. The Ultimate Bar Pass Rate for the school, which the ABA defines as the passage rate for graduates who sat for bar examinations within two years of graduating, was 80.51% for the class of 2021.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-15)

## Employment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Employment")]

According to the school's official [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association")-required disclosures for 2023 graduates, within 10 months after graduation 196 (67.59%) of the 290-member graduating class were employed in full-time positions requiring bar passage (i.e. as attorneys) and 17 (5.86%) were employed in full-time JD advantage positions. Attorney positions were in various size law firms, most in 1–10-attorney firms but some in firms exceeding 500 attorneys; 10 graduates obtained local or state judicial clerkships and four obtained federal clerkships. Seventy-five of the class were otherwise employed in public interest, government, higher education, or business. Seventy-two members (24.83%) were unemployed or employed short–term or part–time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-16)

# UIC drops John Marshall name, citing slave-owning past

By[Mike Stetz](https://nationaljurist.com/author/mike-stetz/)

June 1, 2021

Share

[Copy URL](https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/ "Copy URL")[Email](mailto:?subject=UIC%20drops%20John%20Marshall%20name,%20citing%20slave-owning%20past&body=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/ "Email")[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnationaljurist.com%2Fuic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past%2F "Facebook")[X](https://x.com/intent/post?text=UIC+drops+John+Marshall+name%2C+citing+slave-owning+past&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnationaljurist.com%2Fuic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past%2F&via=DeBusinessTimes "X")[Linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/&title=UIC+drops+John+Marshall+name%2C+citing+slave-owning+past "Linkedin")[ReddIt](https://reddit.com/submit?url=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/&title=UIC+drops+John+Marshall+name%2C+citing+slave-owning+past "ReddIt")

[](https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/# "More")

![Image 3: Building entrance canopy with gold lettering that reads ](https://assets.nationaljurist.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/john-marshall-.jpeg)

When John Marshall Law School in Chicago merged with the University of Illinois at Chicago in 2019, it kept the John Marshall name. It was not a controversial move, given that Marshall is considered one of the greatest Supreme Court justices of all time and the law school had used the name since its founding in 1899.

Then came the killing of George Floyd and the movement that it spurred. Since then institutions have rethought whether they should carry the names of historic figures with stained backgrounds.

Marshall was a slave owner, but felt it was “against natural law” and opposed the slave trade. He was also opposed to large scale emancipation and instead supported sending slaves to Liberia.

The law school formed a task force to weigh in on the name of the school. By a six to one vote, it advised the university to drop Marshall’s name, noting “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the Law School.”

- Advertisement -

The law school will now be called University of Illinois Chicago School of Law.

“The university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” said UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis in a statement.

That still leaves two law schools named after Marshall: Atlanta’s John Marshall and Cleveland Marshall College of Law.

A spokesperson for Atlanta’s John Marshall said of the move: “Our Board of Directors is aware of UIC John Marshall’s decision and has no further comment at this time.”

- Advertisement -

Cleveland Marshall declined to comment. Earlier, it announced it was forming a law school name committee to look into the appropriateness of the name.

The school said at the time: “Removing “Marshall” from our law school’s name would be a very consequential decision by the College of Law and Cleveland State University that will require careful study and thoughtful consideration of different viewpoints from our entire law school and university community.”

It didn’t say when a decision was likely. The committee is operating and holding forums on the subject.

On its website, the school said: “These forums are not intended to directly deal with the question of whether we should change our name or to advocate for any particular viewpoint. Rather, the purpose is to better understand how historians view institutional name changes and how other institutions have approached similar issues. The forums will intentionally present differing views and opinions on this subject.”

- Advertisement -

On change.org, a petition is calling for all schools named after Marshall, which include the three law schools and 15 others, to change their names. It has been signed by 1,500 people.

The petition, initiated by Cleveland-based attorney Hanna Kassis, reads:

“We believe John Marshall’s _true self_– which ‘scholars’ denied us the history of knowing – is inconsistent with our ethos. Therefore, Marshall institutions need to rename. Whether they do or not is ultimately on them, but Marshall institutions need to _honestly evaluate their role in perpetuating systemic racism, be it conscious or unconscious_.”

However, some question the move. A Chicago Tribune editorial argued few from Marshall’s time could pass muster:

“But Marshall was hardly unique in his racial views or his participation in the system of human bondage. There is no purity test from our era he would survive; nor should we expect him to. George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and even Alexander Hamilton owned slaves, and the Constitution provided for the indefinite preservation of the ‘peculiar institution.’ But those founders are rightly revered for achievements that loom larger than their failures.”

# University of Illinois Chicago Strips the Name of John Marshall From Its Law School

May 26, 2021

![Image 8](https://jbhe.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/marshall.jpg)The University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School will change its name to the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law. The John Marshall Law School, formerly an independent law school that was established in 1899, merged with the University of Illinois Chicago in 2019 to create UIC John Marshall Law School. John Marshall served as Chief Justice of the United States from 1801 to 1835.

A university task force encharged with examining the life of John Marshall noted, “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the law school.”

“The name of the school has changed, but it doesn’t erase its proud history or the impact of its faculty, alumni and students. As Chicago’s first and only public law school, our mission continues to center on academic excellence, diversity, student success, and bettering the lives of the people of Chicago and beyond,” said Darby Dickerson, dean of the law school.

Michael Amiridis, chancellor of the University of Illinois Chicago, added that “the university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice, and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,”

### 315 SOUTH PLYMOUTH COURT, CHICAGO, IL 60604

[The John Marshall Law School](https://jmls.uic.edu/) was founded in 1899. The school was named for the influential nineteenth century U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Marshall. The John Marshall Law School, called “Chicago’s law school” by Mayor Richard M. Daley, offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and by offering January enrollment, choices most law schools no longer offer. John Marshall is located in Chicago’s central financial and legal district, most commonly known as [The Loop](https://www.student-space.com/the-loop). It is across the street from the Dirksen Federal Building, which houses the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit and the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, and about four blocks from the Daley Center, which houses the Cook County Courts.

# Board approves new name for UIC Law

May 20, 2021

[![Image 7: UIC School of Law logo](https://today.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/COL.LAW_.LOCKB_.SM_.RGB_.JPG-750wide-390x164.jpg)](https://today.uic.edu/uic_law_informal_lockup-logo-full-color-rgb_uic_law_informal_loc)

The UIC John Marshall Law School will change its name to the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law after receiving approval from the University of Illinois Board of Trustees today.

With all required approvals and agreements obtained in accordance with university processes and contractual obligations with the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation (the successor legal entities that owned and operated the law school, and fund-raised for the school, before it became a part of UIC), the name change will be effective July 1, 2021.

The vote comes after months of review by a task force that gathered input from students, faculty, staff, and alumni, conducted research and proposed principles to guide the institution in evaluating a potential name change.

The task force report noted, “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the Law School.”

“The university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” said UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis.

Following the task force’s report in February and its 6-1 membership recommendation to rename the school, law school faculty voted in favor of a new official name in March. Approval from the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation was received last week by the University of Illinois System.

The John Marshall Law School, formerly an independent law school that was established in 1899, merged with UIC in 2019 to create UIC John Marshall Law School. Since its founding, the school has upheld a tradition of diversity, innovation and opportunity and consistently provided an education that combined an understanding of the theory, philosophy and practice of law.

“The name of the school has changed, but it doesn’t erase its proud history or the impact of its faculty, alumni and students. As Chicago’s first and only public law school, our mission continues to center on academic excellence, diversity, student success and bettering the lives of the people of Chicago and beyond,” said Darby Dickerson, dean of the Law School.

To learn more about the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, which is based at Jackson and State streets in the heart of the Loop and the city’s legal district, visit [go.uic.edu/uiclaw](http://go.uic.edu/uiclaw).

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. # UIC drops John Marshall name, citing slave-owning past

By[Mike Stetz](link_25)

June 1, 2021

Share

[Copy URL](https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/ "Copy URL")[Email](mailto:?subject=UIC%20drops%20John%20Marshall%20name,%20citing%20slave-owning%20past&body=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/ "Email")[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnationaljurist.com%2Fuic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past%2F "Facebook")[X](link_26)[Linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/&title=UIC+drops+John+Marshall+name%2C+citing+slave-owning+past "Linkedin")[ReddIt](https://reddit.com/submit?url=https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/&title=UIC+drops+John+Marshall+name%2C+citing+slave-owning+past "ReddIt")

[](https://nationaljurist.com/uic-drops-john-marshall-name-citing-slave-owning-past/# "More")

![Image 3: Building entrance canopy with gold lettering that reads ](https://assets.nationaljurist.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/john-marshall-.jpeg)

When John Marshall Law School in Chicago merged with the University of Illinois at Chicago in 2019, it kept the John Marshall name. It was not a controversial move, given that Marshall is considered one of the greatest Supreme Court justices of all time and the law school had used the name since its founding in 1899.

Then came the killing of George Floyd and the movement that it spurred. Since then institutions have rethought whether they should carry the names of historic figures with stained backgrounds.

Marshall was a slave owner, but felt it was “against natural law” and opposed the slave trade. He was also opposed to large scale emancipation and instead supported sending slaves to Liberia.

The law school formed a task force to weigh in on the name of the school. By a six to one vote, it advised the university to drop Marshall’s name, noting “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the Law School.”

- Advertisement -

The law school will now be called University of Illinois Chicago School of Law.

“The university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” said UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis in a statement.

That still leaves two law schools named after Marshall: Atlanta’s John Marshall and Cleveland Marshall College of Law.

A spokesperson for Atlanta’s John Marshall said of the move: “Our Board of Directors is aware of UIC John Marshall’s decision and has no further comment at this time.”

- Advertisement -

Cleveland Marshall declined to comment. Earlier, it announced it was forming a law school name committee to look into the appropriateness of the name.

The school said at the time: “Removing “Marshall” from our law school’s name would be a very consequential decision by the College of Law and Cleveland State University that will require careful study and thoughtful consideration of different viewpoints from our entire law school and university community.”

It didn’t say when a decision was likely. The committee is operating and holding forums on the subject.

On its website, the school said: “These forums are not intended to directly deal with the question of whether we should change our name or to advocate for any particular viewpoint. Rather, the purpose is to better understand how historians view institutional name changes and how other institutions have approached similar issues. The forums will intentionally present differing views and opinions on this subject.”

- Advertisement -

On change.org, a petition is calling for all schools named after Marshall, which include the three law schools and 15 others, to change their names. It has been signed by 1,500 people.

The petition, initiated by Cleveland-based attorney Hanna Kassis, reads:

“We believe John Marshall’s _true self_– which ‘scholars’ denied us the history of knowing – is inconsistent with our ethos. Therefore, Marshall institutions need to rename. Whether they do or not is ultimately on them, but Marshall institutions need to _honestly evaluate their role in perpetuating systemic racism, be it conscious or unconscious_.”

However, some question the move. A Chicago Tribune editorial argued few from Marshall’s time could pass muster:

“But Marshall was hardly unique in his racial views or his participation in the system of human bondage. There is no purity test from our era he would survive; nor should we expect him to. George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and even Alexander Hamilton owned slaves, and the Constitution provided for the indefinite preservation of the ‘peculiar institution.’ But those founders are rightly revered for achievements that loom larger than their failures.”

# Board approves new name for UIC Law

May 20, 2021

[![Image 7: UIC School of Law logo](https://today.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/COL.LAW_.LOCKB_.SM_.RGB_.JPG-750wide-390x164.jpg)](https://today.uic.edu/uic_law_informal_lockup-logo-full-color-rgb_uic_law_informal_loc [link_23])

The UIC John Marshall Law School will change its name to the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law after receiving approval from the University of Illinois Board of Trustees today.

With all required approvals and agreements obtained in accordance with university processes and contractual obligations with the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation (the successor legal entities that owned and operated the law school, and fund-raised for the school, before it became a part of UIC), the name change will be effective July 1, 2021.

The vote comes after months of review by a task force that gathered input from students, faculty, staff, and alumni, conducted research and proposed principles to guide the institution in evaluating a potential name change.

The task force report noted, “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the Law School.”

“The university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,” said UIC Chancellor Michael Amiridis.

Following the task force’s report in February and its 6-1 membership recommendation to rename the school, law school faculty voted in favor of a new official name in March. Approval from the Legacy Law School Corporation and the Foundation Legacy Corporation was received last week by the University of Illinois System.

The John Marshall Law School, formerly an independent law school that was established in 1899, merged with UIC in 2019 to create UIC John Marshall Law School. Since its founding, the school has upheld a tradition of diversity, innovation and opportunity and consistently provided an education that combined an understanding of the theory, philosophy and practice of law.

“The name of the school has changed, but it doesn’t erase its proud history or the impact of its faculty, alumni and students. As Chicago’s first and only public law school, our mission continues to center on academic excellence, diversity, student success and bettering the lives of the people of Chicago and beyond,” said Darby Dickerson, dean of the Law School.

To learn more about the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, which is based at Jackson and State streets in the heart of the Loop and the city’s legal district, visit [go.uic.edu/uiclaw](link_24).

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that.  Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active

Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active

# University of Illinois Chicago Strips the Name of John Marshall From Its Law School

May 26, 2021

![Image 8](https://jbhe.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/marshall.jpg)The University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School will change its name to the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law. The John Marshall Law School, formerly an independent law school that was established in 1899, merged with the University of Illinois Chicago in 2019 to create UIC John Marshall Law School. John Marshall served as Chief Justice of the United States from 1801 to 1835.

A university task force encharged with examining the life of John Marshall noted, “that despite Chief Justice Marshall’s legacy as one of the nation’s most significant U.S. Supreme Court justices, the newly discovered research regarding his role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views render him a highly inappropriate namesake for the law school.”

“The name of the school has changed, but it doesn’t erase its proud history or the impact of its faculty, alumni and students. As Chicago’s first and only public law school, our mission continues to center on academic excellence, diversity, student success, and bettering the lives of the people of Chicago and beyond,” said Darby Dickerson, dean of the law school.

Michael Amiridis, chancellor of the University of Illinois Chicago, added that “the university has arrived at this new name following a thorough and carefully studied process that included input from all corners of the institution and beyond, considered issues of racial injustice, and aimed to ensure that our university continues to be a place where diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity are supported and advanced,”

The **University of Illinois Chicago School of Law** (**UIC Law**) is the [law school](link_7) of the [University of Illinois Chicago](link_0), a [public](link_6)[research university](link_15) in [Chicago](link_9), Illinois. Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the **John Marshall Law School** and initially accredited by the [American Bar Association](link_13) in 1951. It merged with the [University of Illinois at Chicago](link_16) in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-4) On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-5) The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6) uncovered by historian [Paul Finkelman](link_17),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-7) had revealed that influential 19th century [U.S. Supreme Court](link_18) chief justice [John Marshall](link_19) was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6)

UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as [The Loop](link_20). It is across the street from the [Dirksen Federal Building](link_21), which houses the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit](link_22) and the [U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois](link_23), and about four blocks from the [Daley Center](link_24), which houses the [Circuit Court of Cook County](link_25) and the Bilandic Building site of the [Illinois Appellate Court](link_26) (First District). The [Chicago Bar Association](link_27) is next door to the law school.

## Admissions and costs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Admissions and costs")]

For the class entering in 2023, UIC Law accepted 69.53% of applicants, with 27.96% of those accepted enrolling. The average enrollee had a 152 [LSAT](link_28) score and 3.39 undergraduate [GPA](link_29).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-Standard_509-1) Tuition and fees at UIC Law for the 2020-2021 academic year is $39,014 for Illinois residents and $48,014 for out of state residents.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-8)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academics")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/John_Marshall_Law.jpg/250px-John_Marshall_Law.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Marshall_Law.jpg)

The former name, John Marshall Law School

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

UIC Law has day and evening divisions, with identical instruction, course content, and scholastic requirements. Lawyering Skills courses, which focus on writing, research, and oral argument, are an integral part of the core curriculum. These courses are taught in small groups, to maximize the individual attention given to each student. A student may earn a J.D. certificate in a certain area of the law or focus more emphatically and earn a joint degree (J.D./LL.M.).

The law school also offers Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Jurisprudence (M.J.) programs for practicing attorneys and non-attorney professionals and other individual students.

UIC School of Law offers seven [Master of Laws](link_30) (LL.M.) programs for attorneys seeking specialized education in legal issues and for current J.D. students who would like the maximum concentration in particular areas of the law. UIC Law offers a comprehensive curriculum in the following areas: Employee Benefits Law, Estate Planning, Information Technology and [Privacy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_Law "Privacy Law"), Intellectual Property Law, International Business and Trade Law, [Real Estate Law](link_31), and Tax Law.

### Journals and organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Journals and organizations")]

There are four honors programs: _UIC Law Review_, _[UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law](link_32)_ ("RIPL"), the [Moot Court](link_33) Honors Program, and the Trial Advocacy & Dispute Resolution Honors Program.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-9) UIC Law sends teams to more than 30 moot court and mock trial competitions annually.

The student community at UIC Law includes more than 50 [student organizations](link_34) engaging in social awareness, community service, legal discussions, and social activities.

The **University of Illinois Chicago** (**UIC**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago") community area of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois, United States.

The university was the second institution established within the [University of Illinois System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System "University of Illinois System") and it is now the largest university in the [Chicago metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_metropolitan_area "Chicago metropolitan area"), having more than 35,000 students[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-6) enrolled in its 16 colleges. It is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Carnegie-7)

### Beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Beginnings")]

The University of Illinois Chicago traces its origins to several health colleges founded during the late 19th century, including the Chicago College of Pharmacy, which opened in 1859, the College of Physicians and Surgeons (1882), and the Columbian College of Dentistry (1893).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Columbian_College_of_Dentistry-8)

The [University of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois "University of Illinois") was chartered in 1867 in [Champaign-Urbana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champaign-Urbana "Champaign-Urbana"), as the state's [land-grant university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university"). In exchange for agreeing to the Champaign-Urbana location, Chicago-area legislators were promised that a "[polytechnical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_technology "Institute of technology")" branch would open in Chicago.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-IIU_established-9) The Chicago-based health colleges affiliated with the university in 1896–97, becoming fully incorporated into the University of Illinois in 1913, as the **Colleges of Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmacy** on Chicago's west side. Medical education and research expanded in the succeeding decades, leading to the development of several other [health science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_science "Health science") colleges, which were brought together as the University of Illinois **Chicago Professional Colleges**. In 1936, the first act of newly elected state representative [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley") was to introduce a resolution calling for the establishment of an undergraduate Chicago campus of the University of Illinois.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10)

### Navy Pier campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Navy Pier campus")]

As [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was drawing to a close, Congress passed the [G.I. Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill "G.I. Bill") in 1944, which sought to reward veterans for their military service. Among other benefits, it provided educational funding, making college degrees far more attainable to a much-wider selection of the American public. In 1945, Daley, who was then a state senator, introduced four bills calling for a university in Chicago.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10) In 1946, realizing that they would be "besieged with applications," University of Illinois officials opened what was to be a temporary branch campus called the **Chicago Undergraduate Division** (CUD) on [Navy Pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Pier "Navy Pier").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11) The campus was not a junior college, but rather had a curriculum based on Urbana's courses, and students who successfully completed the first two years' requirements could go on to Urbana and finish their degree.

Classes at the CUD campus began in October 1946, and approximately 4,000 students enrolled each semester.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-NavyPierHist-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-GIBillHist-13) Nicknamed "[Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard "Harvard") on the rocks," three-quarters of its students were veterans on the [G.I. Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill "G.I. Bill"), many of whom were immigrants and most of whom worked other part-time jobs to support themselves. It also accommodated first-generation college students from working families who commuted from home. (Navy Pier's Undergraduate Division makes an appearance in [Robert Pirsig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Pirsig "Robert Pirsig")'s _[Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zen\_and\_the\_Art\_of\_Motorcycle\_Maintenance "Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance")_; its protagonist taught freshman English there.)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11)

Due to high demand for a public university education in Chicago, the university made plans to create a permanent degree-granting campus in Chicago. Students at CUD generally needed to transfer after two years to a more expensive private college in Chicago,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-14) or go to the [main campus in Champaign–Urbana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign "University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"), where there were fewer opportunities for work, while at the same time as going to school.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11)

### Congress Circle campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Congress Circle campus")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg)

UIC's campus

Daley succeeded in getting the state senate in 1951 to pass a bill calling for a Chicago campus. Daley then became mayor of Chicago in 1955 and pressed the University of Illinois to upgrade the Chicago Undergraduate Center to a full-fledged four-year institution.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10) After a long and controversial site decision process,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-RelocationHist-15) in 1961, Mayor Daley offered the Harrison and [Halsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halsted_Street "Halsted Street") Streets site for the new campus.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCampHist-16) In December 1961, the final decision to establish a four-year university in Chicago was made. In that same year, the Chicago Professional Colleges became the **University of Illinois at the Medical Center** (UIMC).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-auto-17)

Florence Scala led the fight against Mayor Richard J. Daley's plan to demolish her Italian-American neighborhood to construct the campus. In 1963, the trustees of [Hull House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_House "Hull House") accepted an offer of $875,000 for the settlement building. [Jessie Binford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Binford "Jessie Binford") and Scala took the case to the Supreme Court. Scala led marches to protest the construction. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to consider an appeal and the settlement was closed on March 28, 1963. During the construction of the 100-acre (0.40 km 2) UIC campus, 200 businesses and 800 homes were bulldozed in Little Italy, with 5,000 residents displaced.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-18)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-auto-17)

In 1963, construction began on the university's new Chicago campus at Harrison and Halsted Streets south of the [Greektown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greektown,_Chicago "Greektown, Chicago") neighborhood. In February 1965, the new Chicago campus opened and was to be named the **University of Illinois at Congress Circle** (UICC) referencing the nearby [Circle Interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Interchange "Circle Interchange") of [I-290](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_290_(Illinois) "Interstate 290 (Illinois)") and [I-90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_90_in_Illinois "Interstate 90 in Illinois")/[I-94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_Illinois "Interstate 94 in Illinois")).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCamp2Hist-19) Shortly before opening, the Congress Expressway was renamed the Eisenhower Expressway and the interchange Chicago Circle, so the campus was renamed to **University of Illinois at Chicago Circle** (UICC). UICC was designed in the [brutalist style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture") by [Walter Netsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Netsch "Walter Netsch") of [Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill"), a Chicago-based architectural firm responsible for many of today's tallest skyscrapers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-UICHist-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-UICArchDept-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-encyclopedia_of_chicago-22) Unlike the CUD campus, Circle was a degree-granting institution. Within five years of the campus' opening, in addition to [undergraduate degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_degrees "Undergraduate degrees"), virtually every department offered [graduate degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduate_degrees "Graduate degrees").

### Consolidation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Consolidation")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_%2851575326034%29.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_%2851575326034%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_(51575326034).jpg)

The university absorbed the [School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law "University of Illinois Chicago School of Law") in 2019.

In September 1982, the University of Illinois system consolidated UICC and UIMC to form the _University of Illinois at Chicago_ (**UIC**), later dropping the "at" in 2020[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Writing_Style_Guide_-_University_of_Illinois_System-23) to become **University of Illinois Chicago**.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCamp3Hist-24)

In 2000, UIC began developing the south campus. The expansion of UIC south of [Roosevelt Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Road "Roosevelt Road") increased on-campus living space and research facilities.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-When_East_Met_West-25)

In 2015, UIC conducted its first university-wide winter commencements, adding that as a permanent option going forward.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-26)

In 2019, the John Marshall Law School, founded in 1899 and named for the American jurist [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall "John Marshall"), became affiliated with the university.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-27) In 2021, the UI Trustees voted to officially rename UIC John Marshall Law School as [UIC School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law "University of Illinois Chicago School of Law"), citing Marshall's "role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-28)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Campus")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg)

[University Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Hall_(UIC) "University Hall (UIC)"), located on UIC's East Campus

UIC is Chicago's largest university with more than 33,000 students, 12,000 employees, 16 colleges and the state's major public medical center. The East Campus was designed in the [brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist "Brutalist") style by [Walter Netsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Netsch "Walter Netsch").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-29) The plan included second-story walkways that connected all of the buildings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-30) Some of the later buildings in Netsch's design were not rectilinear (the Behavioral Sciences Building) and even irregularly shaped (Science and Engineering South, and the never-completed Art & Architecture building). These demonstrated his idea of "field theory": designs which used squares and rotations of squares superimposed on one another. While the buildings are largely intact, the walkways were taken down in phases during the early 1990s to make the campus more welcoming.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-31) Considerable effort has been expended to modify the original Netsch campus plan to create the feel of a traditional college campus. For example, the area in front of the main administration building, University Hall, has been the site of several renovations in the last decade; and, [Credit Union 1 Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Union_1_Arena "Credit Union 1 Arena") (formerly the UIC Pavilion, a sports arena) was added in 1982.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/UIC_East_Campus.jpg/250px-UIC_East_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_East_Campus.jpg)

A view of the quad from the top floor of University Hall

The East Campus is located on the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago"), just south of [Greektown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greektown,_Chicago "Greektown, Chicago") and a 15-minute walk from [downtown Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). The juxtaposition of campus and commercial density was a direct result of large-scale urban renewal led by Mayor [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-RelocationHist-15)

The Circle Court Shopping Center was a [shopping center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_center "Shopping center") and [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office "Office") complex at 500 South Racine Avenue in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). Completed in 1973, the five-acre property contained 209,600 square feet of space and 350 parking spaces.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-32) In 1990, the University of Illinois authorized negotiations to acquire the property for university use.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-33) By 1993, university records identified it as the Student Services Building and described it as the former Circle Court Shopping Center.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-34) By May 1993, university records referred to the property as the Student Services Building and identified it as the former Circle Court Shopping Center.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-35)

The West Campus, also on the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago"), is much older and includes some buildings built in the [collegiate gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_gothic "Collegiate gothic") style. The colleges of Medicine, Pharmacy, Nursing, Dentistry, Applied Health Sciences and Public Health, as well as the Library of the Health Sciences are all located on the West Campus. The West Campus is in the heart of the [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District "Illinois Medical District") where the [University of Illinois Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Medical_Center "University of Illinois Medical Center") is located.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Platform_at_UIC-Halsted%2C_looking_east.jpg/250px-Platform_at_UIC-Halsted%2C_looking_east.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Platform_at_UIC-Halsted,_looking_east.jpg)

[UIC–Halsted station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC%E2%80%93Halsted_station "UIC–Halsted station") on the [CTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Transit_Authority "Chicago Transit Authority")'s [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(CTA) "Blue Line (CTA)")

The [Chicago Transit Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Transit_Authority "Chicago Transit Authority")'s [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(CTA) "Blue Line (CTA)"), part of the [Chicago 'L'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_'L' "Chicago 'L'"), runs through the median of the [Eisenhower Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenhower_Expressway "Eisenhower Expressway") along the north side of the campus. Three Blue Line stations are close to the university: [UIC-Halsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC-Halsted_(CTA) "UIC-Halsted (CTA)"), [Racine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine_(CTA) "Racine (CTA)"), and [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District_(CTA) "Illinois Medical District (CTA)"). The [Pink Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Line_(CTA) "Pink Line (CTA)") serves UIC's west campus on [Polk Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polk_(CTA) "Polk (CTA)") and runs directly to [the Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Loop_(CTA) "The Loop (CTA)").

### Campus housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Campus housing")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/James_Stukel_Towers.jpg/250px-James_Stukel_Towers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Stukel_Towers.jpg)

UIC's James Stukel Towers residence hall with downtown Chicago and [Willis Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower "Willis Tower") in the background

UIC offers ten residence halls for its students. The East Campus contains five residence halls, the South Campus contains three, and the West Campus contains two. Until the South Campus expansion, UIC students were still predominantly commuters. However, the administration has worked to change the campus to one where most students are residential.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-36) Nearly 6,000 students live within one-and-a-half miles of campus.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-37) 3,800 students, including over half of all freshmen, live in UIC's nine residence halls.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-38) There are also thousands of apartments within walking distance to classes.

On the East Campus, Commons West and Commons South are traditional halls with double rooms opening into a common hallway; each floor shares a common bathroom. Courtyard and Commons North are cluster-style buildings with rooms grouped to share a small private bathroom. These four buildings are connected to the Student Center East which houses a cafeteria, the campus bookstore, a convenience store, bowling/billiards, a barber shop, and the Inner Circle (an assortment of fast food restaurants).

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/UIC_Courtyard_%26_Commons_Dormitory.jpg/250px-UIC_Courtyard_%26_Commons_Dormitory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_Courtyard_&_Commons_Dormitory.jpg)

Courtyard & Commons dormitory buildings on the east campus (next to the building of Architecture, Design, & The Arts)

West Campus housing is composed of the Single Student Residence (SSR, apartments for graduate students) and Polk Street Residence (cluster style rooms). South Campus is home to Marie Robinson Hall and Thomas Beckham Hall, both apartment style buildings. In the fall of 2007, James Stukel Towers opened containing suite style rooms with a bathroom and living room. In keeping with UIC culture, students often refer to residence halls by abbreviations instead of their full names (e.g. "TBH" instead of "Thomas Beckham Hall").

The main purpose of the SSR is to house graduate students, undergraduate students of the ages 24 and older, and professional students. The third and fourth floors house undergraduate students of the ages of 21 through 23. The nursing house is located on the 16th floor. The fifth floor of the SSR has a pilot program for students with families. The program can house up to 15 families.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-SSRDetail-39) Residents of the family program are zoned to [Chicago Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Public_Schools "Chicago Public Schools").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-SSRDetail-39) Families living in the SSR are assigned to Washington Irving Elementary School and [Crane High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_High_School_(Illinois) "Crane High School (Illinois)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-41)

The Academic and Residential Complex, ARC, was opened in response to the ongoing enrollment increase at the university. The building consists of large lecture halls, smaller discussion section classrooms, meeting rooms, and student housing. The building also has a small gym for student occupants and a [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-42)

### Student recreation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Student recreation")]

The UIC Student Recreation Facility (SRF) is a recreational complex for UIC students. Opened in spring 2006, the SRF features a three-story [climbing wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_wall "Climbing wall"), multipurpose courts for games, and a pool with adjoining lazy river. There is also a recreational facility on the west side of the campus. The Sport and Fitness Center, SFC, comprises a fitness floor, Olympic pool, steam room, multipurpose courts, and racquetball courts and much more. UIC Campus Recreation also oversees the Outdoor Field Complex, OFC, on the south side of campus. This outdoor complex comprises two large multipurpose fields.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-43) Campus Recreation hosts a variety of programs that promotes the wellness and well-being of students throughout the academic year. Such events includes RecFest, Destress fest, and many more.

### Medical center and College of Medicine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Medical center and College of Medicine")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg/250px-UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg)

UIC College of Medicine West Tower

The University of Illinois College of Medicine offers a four-year program leading to the MD degree at three different sites in Illinois: Chicago, Peoria, and Rockford. (Urbana-Champaign faculty no longer participate in the University of Illinois College of Medicine, with the establishment of the [Carle Illinois College of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carle_Illinois_College_of_Medicine "Carle Illinois College of Medicine"), hosted entirely at the flagship campus.) UIC is a major part of the [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District "Illinois Medical District") (IMD). While IMD's billing itself "the nation's largest urban medical district" may be up for debate, the district is a major economic force contributing $3.3 billion to the local economy and supporting 50,000 jobs. In popular culture, UIC College of Medicine was the Medical School affiliated with Cook County Hospital in the television series E.R.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Campus renovations")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/UIC_Campus.jpg/250px-UIC_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_Campus.jpg)

Douglass, Grant, and Lincoln Halls with the [Chicago Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop") skyline in the background

After the major $550 million South Campus expansion, the university began renovating existing facilities on campus. This focus is in part due to a constrained state budget: state funds for new buildings are scarce. Since renovation is less costly, this approach is being used to update facilities.

The first such renovations were to three original "pillbox" buildings: Grant Hall, Lincoln Hall, and Douglas Hall.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-44) The renovated buildings use solar and geothermal power which required digging fifty wells 500 feet into the ground east of University Hall. The energy savings of 20–25% led to Lincoln Hall and Douglas Hall being certified US [LEED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design "Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design") Gold. Grant Hall did not apply for LEED certification even though it was the prototype for many of the features found on Lincoln and Douglas Halls.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Lincoln_Hall_sustainability-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Grant_Hall_sustainability-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Douglas_Hall_latest-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-Douglas_Hall_sustainability-48) The new fascia are all glass and the buildings contain facilities for faculty and students. There are plans to expand the renovation project to every lecture hall cluster if the pilot program is successful.

Other campus renovations include the roof of the Behavioral Sciences Building and the terrace of the Education, Performing Arts, and Social Work building.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-49) A brand new building housing the College of Engineering was opened in 2019 to accommodate the increased enrollment in the college. It features the only [high bay structural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_bay_warehouse "High bay warehouse") laboratory in the city of Chicago.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-50)

To accommodate the rising enrollment in the computer science department, a new building is being constructed called the Computer Design Research and Learning Center (CDRLC); it is slated to be completed in the fall of 2024, with a budget of $117.8 million.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago#cite_note-51)
