#### Student government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Student government")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg/250px-%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg)

[Foellinger Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foellinger_Auditorium "Foellinger Auditorium")

U of I has an extensive history of past student governments. Two years after the university opened in 1868, John Milton Gregory and a group of students created a constitution for a student government. Their governance expanded to the entire university in 1873, having a legislative, executive, and judicial branch. For a period of time, this government had the ability to discipline students. In 1883, however, due to a combination of events from Gregory's resignation to student-faculty infighting, the government formally dissolved itself via [plebiscite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebiscite "Plebiscite").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-149)

It was not until 1934, when the Student Senate, the next university-wide student government, was created. A year before, future Illinois Dean of Students, Fred H. Turner and the university's Senate Committee on Student Affairs gave increased power to the Student Council, an organization primarily known for organizing dances. A year after, the Student Council created a constitution and became the Student Senate, under the oversight of the Committee on Student Affairs. This Student Senate would last for 35 years.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-150) The Student Senate changed its purpose and name in 1969, when it became the Undergraduate Student Association (UGSA). It ceased being a representational government, becoming a [collective bargaining agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining_agency "Collective bargaining agency") instead. It often worked with the Graduate Student Association to work on various projects[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-151)

In 1967, [Bruce A. Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_A._Morrison "Bruce A. Morrison") and other U of I graduate founded the Graduate Student Association (GSA). GSA would last until 1978, when it merged with the UGSA to form the Champaign-Urbana Student Association (CUSA).[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-152)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-illinois1948-153) CUSA lasted for only two years when it was replaced by the Student Government Association (SGA) in 1980. SGA lasted for 15 years until it became the Illinois Student Government (ISG) in 1995. ISG lasted until 2004.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-illinois1948-153)

The current university student government, created in 2004, is the Illinois Student Senate, a combined undergraduate and graduate student senate with 54 voting members. The student senators are elected by college and represent the students in the Urbana-Champaign Senate (which comprises both faculty and students), as well as on a variety of faculty and administrative committees, and are led by an internally elected executive board of a president, external vice president, internal vice president, and treasurer. As of 2012[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit), the executive board is supported by an executive staff consisting of a chief of staff, clerk of the Senate, parliamentarian, director of communications, Intern Coordinator, and the historian of the Senate.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-154)

[Busey-Evans Residence Halls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busey-Evans_Residence_Halls "Busey-Evans Residence Halls") is one of many buildings on the [NRHP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRHP "NRHP").

The university provides housing for undergraduates through [24 residence halls in Urbana and Champaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campus_of_the_University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#Residence_halls "Campus of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"). Incoming freshmen are required to live in student housing (campus or certified) their first year on campus. The university also maintains two graduate residence halls, which are restricted to students who are sophomores or above, and three university-owned apartment complexes. Some undergraduates choose to move into apartments or the Greek houses after their first year. There are a number of private dormitories around campus, as well as 15 private, certified residences that partner with the university to offer a variety of different housing options, including ones that are cooperatives, single-gender or religiously affiliated.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-PCH16-155) U of I is known for being one of the first universities to provide accommodations for students with disabilities.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-Education_secretary_UI-156) In 2015, the University of Illinois announced that they would be naming its newest residence hall after [Carlos Montezuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Montezuma "Carlos Montezuma"), also known as Wassaja. He is the first [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") graduate, and is believed to be one of the first Native Americans to receive a medical degree.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-157)

The airport is located in Savoy. Willard Airport is home to university research projects, along with flights from [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"). In 2013, the university's [Institute of Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Institute_of_Aviation "University of Illinois Institute of Aviation") was closed at the University of Illinois and the program was transferred to [Parkland College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkland_College_(United_States) "Parkland College (United States)").

### Security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Security")]

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has a dedicated police department, UIPD, which operates independently from CPD, the department that serves the surrounding Champaign area.

On June 9, 2017, Yingying Zhang, a Chinese international student, was [abducted and murdered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Yingying_Zhang "Murder of Yingying Zhang") in a case that made national headlines at the time. The university subsequently announced plans to install additional, high-definition, security cameras across the campus.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-WQAD8Security-173)

In July 2022, the university announced that it was partnering with local businesses to invest $300,000 to combat violent crime in Champaign County.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-174)

In September 2022, the City of Champaign transferred responsibility for a large swath of Campustown from CPD (Champaign Police Department) to UIPD, claiming that doing so would reduce response times and improve the quality of service. As part of the jurisdictional reforms, the city agreed to pay a substantial portion of the cost to hire seven new officers to patrol the new coverage area.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-175)

Violent crime fell sharply in 2022 compared to the year prior, with shootings and homicides declining by 50 and 47 percent, respectively. The city attributed the decrease in crime to improved staffing levels and the installation of [automatic license plate readers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_number-plate_recognition "Automatic number-plate recognition").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-176)

The university participates in the [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association")'s Division I. The university's athletic teams are known as the Fighting Illini. The university operates a number of athletic facilities, including [Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Stadium_(University_of_Illinois) "Memorial Stadium (University of Illinois)") for [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football"), the [State Farm Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Farm_Center "State Farm Center") for men's and women's basketball, and the Atkins Tennis Center for men's and women's tennis. The men's NCAA basketball team had a dream run in the [2005 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NCAA_Men's_Division_I_Basketball_Tournament "2005 NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Tournament"), with [Bruce Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Weber_(coach) "Bruce Weber (coach)")'s Fighting Illini tying the record for most victories in a season. Their run ended 37–2 with a loss to the [North Carolina Tar Heels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_men's_basketball "North Carolina Tar Heels men's basketball") in the [national championship game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship "NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship"). Illinois is a member of the [Big Ten Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference "Big Ten Conference"). Notable among a number of songs commonly played and sung at various events such as [commencement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduation "Graduation") and [convocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convocation "Convocation"), and athletic games are: [Illinois Loyalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Loyalty "Illinois Loyalty"), the school song; [Oskee Wow Wow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskee_Wow_Wow "Oskee Wow Wow"), the [fight song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fight_song "Fight song"); and [Hail to the Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marching_Illini#Hail_to_the_Orange "Marching Illini"), the alma mater.

On October 15, 1910, the Illinois football team defeated the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") Maroons with a score of 3–0 in a game that Illinois claims was the first [homecoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homecoming "Homecoming") game, though several other schools claim to have held the first homecoming as well.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-177)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-178) On November 10, 2007, the unranked Illinois football team defeated the No. 1 ranked [Ohio State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_State "Ohio State") football team in [Ohio Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Stadium "Ohio Stadium"), the first time that the Illini beat a No. 1 ranked team on the road.

The [University of Illinois Ice Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Ice_Arena "University of Illinois Ice Arena") is home to the university's club [college ice hockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_ice_hockey "College ice hockey") team competing at the [ACHA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Collegiate_Hockey_Association "American Collegiate Hockey Association") level and is also available for recreational use through the Division of Campus Recreation. It was built in 1931 and designed by Chicago architecture firm Holabird and Root, the same firm that designed the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign's Memorial Stadium and Chicago's Soldier Field. It is located on Armory Drive across from the Armory. The structure features four rows of bleacher seating in an elevated balcony that runs the length of the ice rink on either side. These bleachers provide seating for roughly 1,200 fans, with standing room and bench seating available underneath. Because of this set-up the team benches are actually directly underneath the stands.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-179)

In 2015, the university began [Mandarin Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese "Mandarin Chinese") broadcasts of its American football games as a service to its Chinese international students.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-GuardianChinesefootball-134)

The university's division of Disability Resources and Educational Services fields [wheelchair basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Wheelchair_Basketball "University of Illinois Wheelchair Basketball") and wheelchair track teams. Illinois was the first college in the United States to establish a wheelchair basketball team (in 1948) and a women's wheelchair basketball team (in 1970),[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-180) and both the men's and women's teams are members of the intercollegiate divisions of the [National Wheelchair Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Wheelchair_Basketball_Association "National Wheelchair Basketball Association").[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-181) The university is one of ten official training sites for the [United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee"), specializing in [para-athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Para-athletics "Para-athletics").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-182)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-183) The wheelchair programs have been highly successful, producing several [Paralympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralympic "Paralympic") medalists.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-184)

### Mascot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Mascot")]

Main article: [Chief Illiniwek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Illiniwek "Chief Illiniwek")

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Illinois_Fighting_Illini_logo.svg/120px-Illinois_Fighting_Illini_logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illinois_Fighting_Illini_logo.svg)

The [Fighting Illini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Fighting_Illini "Illinois Fighting Illini") athletics logo since 2014[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-185)

The U of I currently has no mascot.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-186)[Chief Illiniwek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Illiniwek "Chief Illiniwek"), also referred to as "The Chief", was from 1926 to 2007 the official symbol of the U of I in university intercollegiate athletic programs. The Chief was typically portrayed by a student dressed in [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") regalia. Several groups protested that the use of a Native American figure and indigenous customs in such a manner was inappropriate and promoted ethnic stereotypes. In August 2005, the National Collegiate Athletic Association expressed disapproval of the university's use of a "hostile or abusive" image.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-LAT2005-187) While initially proposing a consensus approach to the decision about the Chief, the board in 2007 decided that the Chief, its name, image and regalia should be officially retired. Nevertheless, the controversy continues on campus with some students unofficially maintaining the Chief. Complaints continue that indigenous students feel insulted when images of the Chief continue to be present on campus.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-188) The effort to resolve the controversy has included the work of a committee, which issued a report of its "critical conversations" that included over 600 participants representing all sides.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-189)

There is a grassroots campaign of students and alumni to officially recognize the [belted kingfisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belted_kingfisher "Belted kingfisher") as the mascot of the U of I.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-190)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-191) Female belted kingfishers are orange and blue (the school's colors) and the bird is native to Illinois.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-192) A Kingfisher costume has been created and has made appearances on campus.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-193) The campaign to adopt the mascot is not seeking to change the name "Fighting Illini."[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-194) Multiple Indigenous organizations have also expressed support for the Kingfisher.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-195)

Hallene Gateway was dedicated in 1998 by donations from alumni Alan M. and Phyllis Welsh Hallene.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-UIHistories-24)

Twenty-seven alumni and faculty members of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have won a [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize").[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-196)As of 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit), the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign alumni, faculty, and researchers include 24 Nobel laureates (including 11 alumni). In particular, [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") is the only person to have won two Nobel prizes in physics, having done so in 1956 and 1972 while on faculty at the university. In 2003, two faculty members won Nobel prizes in different disciplines: [Paul C. Lauterbur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C._Lauterbur "Paul C. Lauterbur") for physiology or medicine, and [Anthony Leggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Leggett "Anthony Leggett") for physics.

Alumni and faculty have invented the [LED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED") and the [quantum well laser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_well_laser "Quantum well laser") ([Nick Holonyak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Holonyak "Nick Holonyak"), B.S. 1950, M.S. 1951, Ph.D. 1954), [DSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSL "DSL") ([John Cioffi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cioffi "John Cioffi"), B.S. 1978), [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript") ([Brendan Eich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Eich "Brendan Eich"), M.S. 1986),[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-U_of_I_alumn-197) the [integrated circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") ([Jack Kilby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby"), B.S. 1947), the [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") ([John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen"), faculty, 1951–1991), the [pH meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH_meter "PH meter") ([Arnold Beckman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Beckman "Arnold Beckman"), B.S. 1922, M.S. 1923), [MRI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRI "MRI") ([Paul C. Lauterbur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C._Lauterbur "Paul C. Lauterbur")), the [plasma screen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_screen "Plasma screen") ([Donald Bitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Bitzer "Donald Bitzer"), B.S. 1955, M.S. 1956, Ph.D. 1960), color plasma display ([Larry F. Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_F._Weber "Larry F. Weber"), B.S. 1968 M.S. 1971 Ph.D. 1975), the training methodology called PdEI and the coin counter ([James P. Liautaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_P._Liautaud "James P. Liautaud"), B.S. 1963), the statistical algorithm called [Gibbs sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_sampling "Gibbs sampling") in computer vision and the machine learning technique called [random forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forests "Random forests") ([Donald Geman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Geman "Donald Geman"), B.A. 1965), and are responsible for the structural design of such buildings as the [Willis Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower "Willis Tower"), the [John Hancock Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Center "John Hancock Center"), and the [Burj Khalifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burj_Khalifa "Burj Khalifa").[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-198)

Mathematician [Richard Hamming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hamming "Richard Hamming"), known for the [Hamming code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_code "Hamming code") and [Hamming distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance "Hamming distance"), earned a PhD in mathematics from the university's Mathematics Department in 1942.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-199)[Primetime Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award "Primetime Emmy Award")-winning engineer [Alan Bovik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Bovik "Alan Bovik") (B.S. 1980, M.S. 1982, Ph.D. 1984) invented neuroscience-based video quality measurement tools that pervade [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television"), [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media "Social media") and [home cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_cinema "Home cinema").[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-200) Structural engineer [Fazlur Rahman Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fazlur_Rahman_Khan "Fazlur Rahman Khan") earned two master's degrees, and a PhD in structural engineering from the university.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-201)

Illinois alumni and faculty have founded numerous companies and organizations. Notable founders include [Marc Andreessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Andreessen "Marc Andreessen"), co-founder of [Andreessen Horowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz") (2009); [Jerry Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Sanders_(businessman) "Jerry Sanders (businessman)"), co-founder of [AMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMD "AMD") (1969); and [Jerry Colangelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Colangelo "Jerry Colangelo"), founder of the [Arizona Diamondbacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Diamondbacks "Arizona Diamondbacks") (1995). [George Halas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Halas "George Halas"), who founded the [Chicago Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bears "Chicago Bears") (1920) and co-founded the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL "NFL"), and [Reshma Saujani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reshma_Saujani "Reshma Saujani"), founder of [Girls Who Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls_Who_Code "Girls Who Code") (2012), also made significant contributions. In technology, Marc Andreessen and [Brendan Eich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Eich "Brendan Eich") co-founded [Mozilla Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla_Corporation "Mozilla Corporation") and [Netscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netscape "Netscape") in the 1990s, while [Larry Ellison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Ellison "Larry Ellison") and [Bob Miner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Miner "Bob Miner") co-founded [Oracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation") (1977). Other tech innovators include [Nathan Gettings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Gettings "Nathan Gettings") ([Palantir Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palantir_Technologies "Palantir Technologies"), 2003), [Luke Nosek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Nosek "Luke Nosek") and [Max Levchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Levchin "Max Levchin") ([PayPal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PayPal "PayPal"), 1998), [Martin Eberhard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Eberhard "Martin Eberhard") ([Tesla, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. "Tesla, Inc."), 2003), and [Stephen Wolfram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Wolfram "Stephen Wolfram") and [Theodore Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Gray "Theodore Gray") ([Wolfram Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfram_Research "Wolfram Research"), 1987). Additionally, [Hugh Hefner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hefner "Hugh Hefner") founded [Playboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboy "Playboy") Enterprises (1953), [Thomas Siebel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Siebel "Thomas Siebel") co-founded [Siebel Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siebel_Systems "Siebel Systems") (1993), and [Jerry Yue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Yue "Jerry Yue") founded Brain Technologies, Inc. (2010). Other prominent companies like [Yelp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yelp "Yelp") (2004) and [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") (2005) were co-founded by [Jeremy Stoppelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Stoppelman "Jeremy Stoppelman"), [Russel Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russel_Simmons "Russel Simmons"), [Steve Chen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Chen "Steve Chen"), and [Jawed Karim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawed_Karim "Jawed Karim").[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-202)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-203)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-204) Alumni have also led several companies, including [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's"), [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"), [BP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BP "BP"), [Kodak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastman_Kodak "Eastman Kodak"), [Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_Oil "Shell Oil"), [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors"), [AT&T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T "AT&T"), and [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") and others.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#cite_note-U_of_I_alumn-197)

# Appointments & Awards

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/four-black-scholars-selected-for-new-faculty-roles/ "Four Black Women Selected for New Faculty Roles")

### [Four Black Women Selected for New Faculty Roles](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/four-black-scholars-selected-for-new-faculty-roles/ "Four Black Women Selected for New Faculty Roles")

October 2, 2026

Camille Borders and Sophia Mongero are new assistant professors at Bates College in Maine and Smith College in Massachusetts, respectively. Jametta A. Davis is assistant director of the Hampton University Honors College and Kiana Dibo-Armstrong is chair of the department of social work at Savannah State University.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/keisha-rogers-receives-black-mental-health-educator-of-the-year-award/ "Keisha Rogers Receives Black Mental Health Educator of the Year Award")

### [Keisha Rogers Receives Black Mental Health Educator of the Year Award](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/keisha-rogers-receives-black-mental-health-educator-of-the-year-award/ "Keisha Rogers Receives Black Mental Health Educator of the Year Award")

October 2, 2026

The Black Mental Health Symposium has honored Dr. Rogers, professor of rehabilitation counseling at Winston-Salem State University, for her contributions to counselor education, mentorship, and advocacy.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/five-black-americans-appointed-to-administrative-roles-at-hbcus/ "Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs")

### [Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/five-black-americans-appointed-to-administrative-roles-at-hbcus/ "Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs")

October 2, 2026

# Appointments & Awards

[](link_12)

### [Four Black Women Selected for New Faculty Roles](link_12)

October 2, 2026

Camille Borders and Sophia Mongero are new assistant professors at Bates College in Maine and Smith College in Massachusetts, respectively. Jametta A. Davis is assistant director of the Hampton University Honors College and Kiana Dibo-Armstrong is chair of the department of social work at Savannah State University.

[](link_13)

### [Keisha Rogers Receives Black Mental Health Educator of the Year Award](link_13)

October 2, 2026

The Black Mental Health Symposium has honored Dr. Rogers, professor of rehabilitation counseling at Winston-Salem State University, for her contributions to counselor education, mentorship, and advocacy.

[](link_14)

### [Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs](link_14)

October 2, 2026

The appointments are Kristi L. Smith at the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff, Alicia Williams at Grambling State University, Octavius Rice at Johnson C. Smith University, Abiodun Durojaye at Howard University, and Joshua Busby at Langston University.

[](link_15)

### [Five Black Scholars Selected for New Faculty Roles](link_15)

September 25, 2026

Camille A. Brown was named to an endowed professorship in dance at the University of Southern California. Robert R. Lindsey of Johnson C. Smith University and Ashley Leak Bryant of the University of North Carolina are taking on new leadership roles. Amaryah Shaye Armstrong and Tré Watkins are new assistant professors at Columbia university and Point Loma Nazarene University, respectively.

[](link_16)

### [Prudence Carter Receives Career Award From the American Sociological Association](link_16)

September 25, 2026

A leading sociologist of education, Dr. Carter currently serves as an endowed professor and director of the Center for the Study of Race and Ethnicity in America at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island. 

[](link_17)

### [A Trio of Black Administrators Selected for New Roles in Academia](link_17)

September 25, 2026

Blair Lee is the inaugural associate vice president and chief marketing and communications officer at Front Range Community College in Colorado. Atia Garrett-Washington was appointed vice president of enrollment management at Dillard University in New Orleans, and Elmore J. Jones, Jr. was appointed compliance officer at Hampton University in Virginia.

[](link_18)

### [Five Black Scholars Appointed to New Roles](link_18)

September 18, 2026

Ezemenari M. Obasi of Wayne State University has been appointed to the National Advisory Council on Minority Health and Health Disparities. Miriam Johnson, Judith Crocker-Billingsley, and Lewis Johnson are taking on new academic leadership roles at universities. Scott Poulson-Bryant joined the faculty of the New York University Tisch School of the Arts.

[](link_19)

### [Tomikia LeGrande Honored by the Thurgood Marshall College Fund](link_19)

September 18, 2026

Dr. LeGrande became the ninth president of Prairie View A&M University in June 2023. Earlier in her career, she held key leadership roles in enrollment management at Virginia Commonwealth University and the University of Houston-Downtown.

[](link_20)

### [New Roles for Four Black Administrators in Higher Education](link_20)

September 18, 2026

The administrators who are taking on new roles in higher education are Johnnie Watson III at Howard University, Wesley Fountain at Fayetteville State University, Felicia Ellzy-Smith at Dutchess Community College, and Jordan M. Davis at the University of Cincinnati.

[](link_21)

### [UNC-Chapel Hill to Name New Residence Hall After Pioneering Black Faculty](link_21)

September 15, 2026

The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill's new Jackson Hall honors two of the university's earliest Black professors. Blyden Jackson was the university's first tenured Black faculty member and his wife Roberta was the first Black tenure-track faculty member in the School of Education.

[](link_22)

### [New Academic Appointments for Eight Black Scholars](link_22)

September 11, 2026

Here is this week’s roundup of Black faculty members who have been appointed to new positions in the academic world. If you have news for our appointments section, please email the information to contact@jbhe.com. 

[](link_23)

### [UCLA’s E. Dale Abel Receives Prestigious Honor from the Government of Jamaica](link_23)

September 11, 2026

E. Dale Abel of the University of California, Los Angles has been awarded the Order of Distinction in the Rank of Commander by the Government of Jamaica. The award is one of the nation's highest honors.

[](link_24)

### [Three Black Administrators Appointed to New Roles in Higher Education](link_24)

September 11, 2026

Lindsey Hunter is the vice president for strategic enrollment management at Langston University in Oklahoma. LaShaunda Reese is a new associate director in the Institute for Black Catholic Studies at Xavier University of Louisiana and Darrell L. Farewell is chief financial officer at Salem Academy and College in North Carolina.

[](link_25)

### [New Faculty Roles for Six Black Scholars in Higher Education](link_25)

September 4, 2026

The faculty appointments are Heather Tookes at Yale University, Yaa Oparebea Ampofo at Columbia University, Curtis R. Govan, Jr., II at Jarvis Christian University, Shaun Ossei-Owusu at the University of California College of Law, San Francisco, Arnold Holland at California State University, Fullerton, and Lyrric Jackson at Spelman College. 

[](link_26)

### [Deborah Willis Selected to Receive an American Book Award](link_26)

September 4, 2026

Deborah Willis is a University Professor and chair of the department of photography and imaging at the Tisch School of the Arts at New York University. She will be presented with an American Book Award on September 28.

[](link_27)

### [Four Black Administrators Selected for Key Leadership Roles at Universities](link_27)

September 4, 2026

Alton C. Standifer is chief of staff at Clemson University in South Carolina and Alfred S. Chandler Jr. is chief of police at Hampton University in Virginia. Tamara White is the inaugural director for belonging and servingness at the University of Northern Colorado and Ashley Robinson is the athletic director at Texas Southern University.

[](link_28)

### [Eight Black Scholars Selected for New Academic Appointments](link_28)

August 28, 2026

The appointments are David W. Brown at Temple University, Christina Baker at the University of California, Merced, Dennis C. Sweet IV at Washington and Lee University, Trena Warren at Belhaven University, Tiffani Chidume at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Avery Bargassé at the University of Cincinnati, Jean Beaman at the City University of New York, and Aimee J. Carlisle at the College of Law at the University of California, San Francisco.

[](link_29)

### [Brittany Suggs Receives Emerging Leader Award From the American Counseling Association](link_29)

August 28, 2026

The American Counseling Association has presented its Robert H. Rencken Emerging Professor Leader Award to Brittany Suggs, an assistant professor and graduate clinical coordinator in the department of counseling and human services at Old Dominion University in Norfolk, Virginia.

[](link_30)

### [New Roles for Four Black Administrators in Higher Education](link_30)

August 28, 2026

Mattie White and Katreshia Louis-Verrett are the new athletic directors at Emory University and North Carolina A&T State University, respectively. Kizzy N. Lea is chief financial officer at Livingstone College and William C. Nelson Jr. is chief of staff to the provost at Virginia Commonwealth University.

[](link_31)

### [New Associate Dean Positions for Three Faculty Members at North Carolina Central University](link_31)

August 21, 2026

At North Carolina Central University, Tryan L. McMickens is a new associate dean in the School of Education. Katrina Smith and Nakia Davis are taking on associate dean roles in the School of Law.

[](link_32)

### [Yale’s Mae-ling Lokko Recognized for Her Work in Architectural Design](link_32)

August 21, 2026

Dr. Lokko focuses her work on the intersectoral design and research of bio-based materials to drive ecological health and generative justice goals. She currently serves as an assistant professor in the School of Architecture and assistant director of the Center for Ecosystems in Architecture at Yale University.

[](link_33)

### [New Roles for Ten Black Administrators at Colleges and Universities](link_33)

August 21, 2026

Here is this week’s roundup of African Americans who have been appointed to new administrative positions at colleges and universities throughout the United States. If you have news for our appointments section, please email the information to contact@jbhe.com.

[](link_34)

### [Nwando Achebe Elected to the Royal Historical Society](link_34)

August 18, 2026

Dr. Achebe, an endowed professor at Michigan State University, is known for her research on the study of women, gender, sexuality, and oral history in Nigeria.

[](link_35)

### [NACUBO Presents Its Highest Honor to Dawn Rhodes](link_35)

August 14, 2026

The National Association of College and University Business Officers is honoring Dawn Rhodes, chief business and finance officer and senior vice president at the University of Maryland, Baltimore.

[](link_36)

### [New Roles for Four Black Scholars in Academia](link_36)

August 14, 2026

Daniel Hastings has been granted the highest faculty honor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Linda Baker of Southern Illinois University Carbondale and Derrick Cohens of the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff are taking on leadership roles at their institutions. Florida State University's Alma Littles is the new president of the Florida Medical Association.

[](link_37)

### [Shatema Threadcraft Receives Book Awards From the American Political Science Association](link_37)

August 14, 2026

Dr. Threadcraft is a member of the Vanderbilt University faculty. Her new book, _The Labors of Resurrection: Black Women, Necromancy, and Morr

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/racial-differences-in-how-long-students-take-to-earn-an-undergraduate-degree/ "Racial Differences in How Long Students Take to Earn an Undergraduate Degree")

### [Racial Differences in How Long Students Take to Earn an Undergraduate Degree](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/racial-differences-in-how-long-students-take-to-earn-an-undergraduate-degree/ "Racial Differences in How Long Students Take to Earn an Undergraduate Degree")

October 5, 2026

Among Black students who earned an undergraduate award (bachelor's degrees, associate degrees, or certificates) in 2024–2025, those attending HBCUs completed their program faster than those attending other institutions.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/bowie-state-university-to-lay-off-20-faculty-members/ "Bowie State University to Lay Off 20 Faculty Members")

### [Bowie State University to Lay Off 20 Faculty Members](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/bowie-state-university-to-lay-off-20-faculty-members/ "Bowie State University to Lay Off 20 Faculty Members")

October 2, 2026

Bowie State University plans to cut 20 faculty positions by the start of fiscal year 2028. These layoffs follow the HBCU's decision to cut 79 staff positions during the Spring 2026 semester in an effort to alleviate its $18 million deficit ahead of fiscal year 2027.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/savannah-state-university-launches-the-john-lewis-school-of-public-policy-and-social-sciences/ "Savannah State University Launches the John Lewis School of Public Policy and Social Sciences")

### [Savannah State University Launches the John Lewis School of Public Policy and Social Sciences](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/savannah-state-university-launches-the-john-lewis-school-of-public-policy-and-social-sciences/ "Savannah State University Launches the John Lewis School of Public Policy and Social Sciences")

October 2, 2026

The John Lewis School of Public Policy and Social Sciences will serve as the new home for undergraduate and graduate programs in behavior analysis, criminal justice, homeland security and emergency management, political science, sociology, and social work.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/morehouse-college-opens-new-multimedia-center-with-support-from-michael-jordan/ "Morehouse College Opens New Multimedia Center With Support From Michael Jordan")

### [Morehouse College Opens New Multimedia Center With Support From Michael Jordan](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/morehouse-college-opens-new-multimedia-center-with-support-from-michael-jordan/ "Morehouse College Opens New Multimedia Center With Support From Michael Jordan")

October 2, 2026

Housed in the HBCU's journalism in sports, culture, and social justice department, the Morehouse Multimedia Center will serve as a hub for creative productions, digital storytelling, sports broadcasting, podcasting, filmmaking, and projects developed with emerging media technologies.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/five-black-americans-appointed-to-administrative-roles-at-hbcus/ "Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs")

### [Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs](https://jbhe.com/2026/10/five-black-americans-appointed-to-administrative-roles-at-hbcus/ "Five Black Americans Appointed to Administrative Roles at HBCUs")

October 2, 2026

The appointments are Kristi L. Smith at the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff, Alicia Williams at Grambling State University, Octavius Rice at Johnson C. Smith University, Abiodun Durojaye at Howard University, and Joshua Busby at Langston University.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/higher-education-gifts-or-grants-of-interest-to-african-americans-122/ "Higher Education Gifts or Grants of Interest to African Americans")

### [Higher Education Gifts or Grants of Interest to African Americans](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/higher-education-gifts-or-grants-of-interest-to-african-americans-122/ "Higher Education Gifts or Grants of Interest to African Americans")

September 30, 2026

Here is this week’s news of grants or gifts to historically Black colleges and universities or for programs of particular interest to African Americans in higher education.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/u-s-news-world-report-names-spelman-college-the-countrys-top-hbcu/ "*U.S. News & World Report* Names Spelman College the Country’s Top HBCU")

### [*U.S. News & World Report* Names Spelman College the Country’s Top HBCU](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/u-s-news-world-report-names-spelman-college-the-countrys-top-hbcu/ "*U.S. News & World Report* Names Spelman College the Country’s Top HBCU")

September 28, 2026

For the twentieth consecutive year, _U.S. News & World Report_ has named Spelman College in Atlanta the best HBCU in the United States. Howard University was second, Tuskegee University was third, Morehouse College was fourth, and North Carolina A&T State University was fifth.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/trump-administration-announces-174-million-investment-to-support-hbcus/ "Trump Administration Announces $174 Million Investment to Support HBCUs")

### [Trump Administration Announces $174 Million Investment to Support HBCUs](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/trump-administration-announces-174-million-investment-to-support-hbcus/ "Trump Administration Announces $174 Million Investment to Support HBCUs")

September 28, 2026

The Trump Administration's latest investment in HBCUs follows a prior investment of $435 million in September 2025. These funds were initially allocated for programs supporting Minority-Serving Institutions, which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions and Predominately Black Institutions.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/honda-announces-10-million-endowment-to-support-hbcus/ "Honda Announces $10 Million Endowment to Support HBCUs")

### [Honda Announces $10 Million Endowment to Support HBCUs](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/honda-announces-10-million-endowment-to-support-hbcus/ "Honda Announces $10 Million Endowment to Support HBCUs")

September 25, 2026

Honda's new Drive the Legacy Fund will provide HBCUs with institutional grants that aim to address challenges such as such as chronic underfunding and capital investment gaps, aging physical infrastructure, digital and technology infrastructure deficits, and faculty recruitment and retention challenges.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/four-historically-or-predominately-black-community-colleges-to-participate-in-faculty-training-program/ "Four Historically or Predominately Black Colleges to Participate in Faculty Training Program")

### [Four Historically or Predominately Black Colleges to Participate in Faculty Training Program](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/four-historically-or-predominately-black-community-colleges-to-participate-in-faculty-training-program/ "Four Historically or Predominately Black Colleges to Participate in Faculty Training Program")

September 25, 2026

Complete College America and the Association of College and University Educators are bringing a new training program to faculty at Lawson State Community College, Coahoma Community College, Baton Rouge Community College, and Delgado Community College.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/two-south-carolina-hbcus-establish-new-transfer-pathway-program/ "Two South Carolina HBCUs Establish New Transfer Pathway Program")

### [Two South Carolina HBCUs Establish New Transfer Pathway Program](https://jbhe.com/2026/09/two-south-carolina-hbcus-establish-new-transfer-pathway-program/ "Two South Carolina HBCUs Establish New Transfer Pathway Program")

September 25, 2026

The **University of Illinois Chicago** (**UIC**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago") community area of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois, United States.

The university was the second institution established within the [University of Illinois System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_System "University of Illinois System") and it is now the largest university in the [Chicago metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_metropolitan_area "Chicago metropolitan area"), having more than 35,000 students[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-6) enrolled in its 16 colleges. It is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Carnegie-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Catalog_%281963%29_%2814592057920%29.jpg/250px-Catalog_%281963%29_%2814592057920%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Catalog_(1963)_(14592057920).jpg)

### Beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Beginnings")]

The University of Illinois Chicago traces its origins to several health colleges founded during the late 19th century, including the Chicago College of Pharmacy, which opened in 1859, the College of Physicians and Surgeons (1882), and the Columbian College of Dentistry (1893).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Columbian_College_of_Dentistry-8)

The [University of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois "University of Illinois") was chartered in 1867 in [Champaign-Urbana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champaign-Urbana "Champaign-Urbana"), as the state's [land-grant university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university"). In exchange for agreeing to the Champaign-Urbana location, Chicago-area legislators were promised that a "[polytechnical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_technology "Institute of technology")" branch would open in Chicago.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-IIU_established-9) The Chicago-based health colleges affiliated with the university in 1896–97, becoming fully incorporated into the University of Illinois in 1913, as the **Colleges of Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmacy** on Chicago's west side. Medical education and research expanded in the succeeding decades, leading to the development of several other [health science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_science "Health science") colleges, which were brought together as the University of Illinois **Chicago Professional Colleges**. In 1936, the first act of newly elected state representative [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley") was to introduce a resolution calling for the establishment of an undergraduate Chicago campus of the University of Illinois.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10)

### Navy Pier campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Navy Pier campus")]

As [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was drawing to a close, Congress passed the [G.I. Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill "G.I. Bill") in 1944, which sought to reward veterans for their military service. Among other benefits, it provided educational funding, making college degrees far more attainable to a much-wider selection of the American public. In 1945, Daley, who was then a state senator, introduced four bills calling for a university in Chicago.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10) In 1946, realizing that they would be "besieged with applications," University of Illinois officials opened what was to be a temporary branch campus called the **Chicago Undergraduate Division** (CUD) on [Navy Pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Pier "Navy Pier").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11) The campus was not a junior college, but rather had a curriculum based on Urbana's courses, and students who successfully completed the first two years' requirements could go on to Urbana and finish their degree.

Classes at the CUD campus began in October 1946, and approximately 4,000 students enrolled each semester.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-NavyPierHist-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-GIBillHist-13) Nicknamed "[Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard "Harvard") on the rocks," three-quarters of its students were veterans on the [G.I. Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill "G.I. Bill"), many of whom were immigrants and most of whom worked other part-time jobs to support themselves. It also accommodated first-generation college students from working families who commuted from home. (Navy Pier's Undergraduate Division makes an appearance in [Robert Pirsig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Pirsig "Robert Pirsig")'s _[Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zen\_and\_the\_Art\_of\_Motorcycle\_Maintenance "Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance")_; its protagonist taught freshman English there.)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11)

Due to high demand for a public university education in Chicago, the university made plans to create a permanent degree-granting campus in Chicago. Students at CUD generally needed to transfer after two years to a more expensive private college in Chicago,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-14) or go to the [main campus in Champaign–Urbana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign "University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"), where there were fewer opportunities for work, while at the same time as going to school.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-pier-11)

### Congress Circle campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Congress Circle campus")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-2.jpg)

UIC's campus

Daley succeeded in getting the state senate in 1951 to pass a bill calling for a Chicago campus. Daley then became mayor of Chicago in 1955 and pressed the University of Illinois to upgrade the Chicago Undergraduate Center to a full-fledged four-year institution.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Daley_for_UIC-10) After a long and controversial site decision process,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-RelocationHist-15) in 1961, Mayor Daley offered the Harrison and [Halsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halsted_Street "Halsted Street") Streets site for the new campus.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCampHist-16) In December 1961, the final decision to establish a four-year university in Chicago was made. In that same year, the Chicago Professional Colleges became the **University of Illinois at the Medical Center** (UIMC).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-auto-17)

Florence Scala led the fight against Mayor Richard J. Daley's plan to demolish her Italian-American neighborhood to construct the campus. In 1963, the trustees of [Hull House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_House "Hull House") accepted an offer of $875,000 for the settlement building. [Jessie Binford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Binford "Jessie Binford") and Scala took the case to the Supreme Court. Scala led marches to protest the construction. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to consider an appeal and the settlement was closed on March 28, 1963. During the construction of the 100-acre (0.40 km 2) UIC campus, 200 businesses and 800 homes were bulldozed in Little Italy, with 5,000 residents displaced.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-18)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-auto-17)

In 1963, construction began on the university's new Chicago campus at Harrison and Halsted Streets south of the [Greektown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greektown,_Chicago "Greektown, Chicago") neighborhood. In February 1965, the new Chicago campus opened and was to be named the **University of Illinois at Congress Circle** (UICC) referencing the nearby [Circle Interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Interchange "Circle Interchange") of [I-290](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_290_(Illinois) "Interstate 290 (Illinois)") and [I-90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_90_in_Illinois "Interstate 90 in Illinois")/[I-94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_Illinois "Interstate 94 in Illinois")).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCamp2Hist-19) Shortly before opening, the Congress Expressway was renamed the Eisenhower Expressway and the interchange Chicago Circle, so the campus was renamed to **University of Illinois at Chicago Circle** (UICC). UICC was designed in the [brutalist style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture") by [Walter Netsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Netsch "Walter Netsch") of [Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill"), a Chicago-based architectural firm responsible for many of today's tallest skyscrapers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-UICHist-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-UICArchDept-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-encyclopedia_of_chicago-22) Unlike the CUD campus, Circle was a degree-granting institution. Within five years of the campus' opening, in addition to [undergraduate degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_degrees "Undergraduate degrees"), virtually every department offered [graduate degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduate_degrees "Graduate degrees").

### Consolidation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Consolidation")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_%2851575326034%29.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_%2851575326034%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law_(51575326034).jpg)

The university absorbed the [School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law "University of Illinois Chicago School of Law") in 2019.

In September 1982, the University of Illinois system consolidated UICC and UIMC to form the _University of Illinois at Chicago_ (**UIC**), later dropping the "at" in 2020[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Writing_Style_Guide_-_University_of_Illinois_System-23) to become **University of Illinois Chicago**.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-CircleCamp3Hist-24)

In 2000, UIC began developing the south campus. The expansion of UIC south of [Roosevelt Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Road "Roosevelt Road") increased on-campus living space and research facilities.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-When_East_Met_West-25)

In 2015, UIC conducted its first university-wide winter commencements, adding that as a permanent option going forward.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-26)

In 2019, the John Marshall Law School, founded in 1899 and named for the American jurist [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall "John Marshall"), became affiliated with the university.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-27) In 2021, the UI Trustees voted to officially rename UIC John Marshall Law School as [UIC School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law "University of Illinois Chicago School of Law"), citing Marshall's "role as a slave trader, slave owner of hundreds of slaves, pro-slavery jurisprudence, and racist views."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-28)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Campus")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg/250px-University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago_-1.jpg)

[University Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Hall_(UIC) "University Hall (UIC)"), located on UIC's East Campus

UIC is Chicago's largest university with more than 33,000 students, 12,000 employees, 16 colleges and the state's major public medical center. The East Campus was designed in the [brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist "Brutalist") style by [Walter Netsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Netsch "Walter Netsch").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-29) The plan included second-story walkways that connected all of the buildings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-30) Some of the later buildings in Netsch's design were not rectilinear (the Behavioral Sciences Building) and even irregularly shaped (Science and Engineering South, and the never-completed Art & Architecture building). These demonstrated his idea of "field theory": designs which used squares and rotations of squares superimposed on one another. While the buildings are largely intact, the walkways were taken down in phases during the early 1990s to make the campus more welcoming.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-31) Considerable effort has been expended to modify the original Netsch campus plan to create the feel of a traditional college campus. For example, the area in front of the main administration building, University Hall, has been the site of several renovations in the last decade; and, [Credit Union 1 Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Union_1_Arena "Credit Union 1 Arena") (formerly the UIC Pavilion, a sports arena) was added in 1982.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/UIC_East_Campus.jpg/250px-UIC_East_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_East_Campus.jpg)

A view of the quad from the top floor of University Hall

The East Campus is located on the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago"), just south of [Greektown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greektown,_Chicago "Greektown, Chicago") and a 15-minute walk from [downtown Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). The juxtaposition of campus and commercial density was a direct result of large-scale urban renewal led by Mayor [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-RelocationHist-15)

The Circle Court Shopping Center was a [shopping center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_center "Shopping center") and [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office "Office") complex at 500 South Racine Avenue in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). Completed in 1973, the five-acre property contained 209,600 square feet of space and 350 parking spaces.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-32) In 1990, the University of Illinois authorized negotiations to acquire the property for university use.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-33) By 1993, university records identified it as the Student Services Building and described it as the former Circle Court Shopping Center.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-34) By May 1993, university records referred to the property as the Student Services Building and identified it as the former Circle Court Shopping Center.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-35)

The West Campus, also on the [Near West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_West_Side,_Chicago "Near West Side, Chicago"), is much older and includes some buildings built in the [collegiate gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_gothic "Collegiate gothic") style. The colleges of Medicine, Pharmacy, Nursing, Dentistry, Applied Health Sciences and Public Health, as well as the Library of the Health Sciences are all located on the West Campus. The West Campus is in the heart of the [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District "Illinois Medical District") where the [University of Illinois Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Medical_Center "University of Illinois Medical Center") is located.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Platform_at_UIC-Halsted%2C_looking_east.jpg/250px-Platform_at_UIC-Halsted%2C_looking_east.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Platform_at_UIC-Halsted,_looking_east.jpg)

[UIC–Halsted station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC%E2%80%93Halsted_station "UIC–Halsted station") on the [CTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Transit_Authority "Chicago Transit Authority")'s [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(CTA) "Blue Line (CTA)")

The [Chicago Transit Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Transit_Authority "Chicago Transit Authority")'s [Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Line_(CTA) "Blue Line (CTA)"), part of the [Chicago 'L'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_'L' "Chicago 'L'"), runs through the median of the [Eisenhower Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenhower_Expressway "Eisenhower Expressway") along the north side of the campus. Three Blue Line stations are close to the university: [UIC-Halsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC-Halsted_(CTA) "UIC-Halsted (CTA)"), [Racine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine_(CTA) "Racine (CTA)"), and [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District_(CTA) "Illinois Medical District (CTA)"). The [Pink Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Line_(CTA) "Pink Line (CTA)") serves UIC's west campus on [Polk Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polk_(CTA) "Polk (CTA)") and runs directly to [the Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Loop_(CTA) "The Loop (CTA)").

### Campus housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Campus housing")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/James_Stukel_Towers.jpg/250px-James_Stukel_Towers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:James_Stukel_Towers.jpg)

UIC's James Stukel Towers residence hall with downtown Chicago and [Willis Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower "Willis Tower") in the background

UIC offers ten residence halls for its students. The East Campus contains five residence halls, the South Campus contains three, and the West Campus contains two. Until the South Campus expansion, UIC students were still predominantly commuters. However, the administration has worked to change the campus to one where most students are residential.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-36) Nearly 6,000 students live within one-and-a-half miles of campus.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-37) 3,800 students, including over half of all freshmen, live in UIC's nine residence halls.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-38) There are also thousands of apartments within walking distance to classes.

On the East Campus, Commons West and Commons South are traditional halls with double rooms opening into a common hallway; each floor shares a common bathroom. Courtyard and Commons North are cluster-style buildings with rooms grouped to share a small private bathroom. These four buildings are connected to the Student Center East which houses a cafeteria, the campus bookstore, a convenience store, bowling/billiards, a barber shop, and the Inner Circle (an assortment of fast food restaurants).

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/UIC_Courtyard_%26_Commons_Dormitory.jpg/250px-UIC_Courtyard_%26_Commons_Dormitory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_Courtyard_&_Commons_Dormitory.jpg)

Courtyard & Commons dormitory buildings on the east campus (next to the building of Architecture, Design, & The Arts)

West Campus housing is composed of the Single Student Residence (SSR, apartments for graduate students) and Polk Street Residence (cluster style rooms). South Campus is home to Marie Robinson Hall and Thomas Beckham Hall, both apartment style buildings. In the fall of 2007, James Stukel Towers opened containing suite style rooms with a bathroom and living room. In keeping with UIC culture, students often refer to residence halls by abbreviations instead of their full names (e.g. "TBH" instead of "Thomas Beckham Hall").

The main purpose of the SSR is to house graduate students, undergraduate students of the ages 24 and older, and professional students. The third and fourth floors house undergraduate students of the ages of 21 through 23. The nursing house is located on the 16th floor. The fifth floor of the SSR has a pilot program for students with families. The program can house up to 15 families.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-SSRDetail-39) Residents of the family program are zoned to [Chicago Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Public_Schools "Chicago Public Schools").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-SSRDetail-39) Families living in the SSR are assigned to Washington Irving Elementary School and [Crane High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_High_School_(Illinois) "Crane High School (Illinois)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-41)

The Academic and Residential Complex, ARC, was opened in response to the ongoing enrollment increase at the university. The building consists of large lecture halls, smaller discussion section classrooms, meeting rooms, and student housing. The building also has a small gym for student occupants and a [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-42)

### Student recreation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Student recreation")]

The UIC Student Recreation Facility (SRF) is a recreational complex for UIC students. Opened in spring 2006, the SRF features a three-story [climbing wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_wall "Climbing wall"), multipurpose courts for games, and a pool with adjoining lazy river. There is also a recreational facility on the west side of the campus. The Sport and Fitness Center, SFC, comprises a fitness floor, Olympic pool, steam room, multipurpose courts, and racquetball courts and much more. UIC Campus Recreation also oversees the Outdoor Field Complex, OFC, on the south side of campus. This outdoor complex comprises two large multipurpose fields.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-43) Campus Recreation hosts a variety of programs that promotes the wellness and well-being of students throughout the academic year. Such events includes RecFest, Destress fest, and many more.

### Medical center and College of Medicine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Medical center and College of Medicine")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg/250px-UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_College_of_Medicine_West_Tower_-_3182467036.jpg)

UIC College of Medicine West Tower

The University of Illinois College of Medicine offers a four-year program leading to the MD degree at three different sites in Illinois: Chicago, Peoria, and Rockford. (Urbana-Champaign faculty no longer participate in the University of Illinois College of Medicine, with the establishment of the [Carle Illinois College of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carle_Illinois_College_of_Medicine "Carle Illinois College of Medicine"), hosted entirely at the flagship campus.) UIC is a major part of the [Illinois Medical District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Medical_District "Illinois Medical District") (IMD). While IMD's billing itself "the nation's largest urban medical district" may be up for debate, the district is a major economic force contributing $3.3 billion to the local economy and supporting 50,000 jobs. In popular culture, UIC College of Medicine was the Medical School affiliated with Cook County Hospital in the television series E.R.

### Campus renovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Campus renovations")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/UIC_Campus.jpg/250px-UIC_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_Campus.jpg)

Douglass, Grant, and Lincoln Halls with the [Chicago Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop") skyline in the background

After the major $550 million South Campus expansion, the university began renovating existing facilities on campus. This focus is in part due to a constrained state budget: state funds for new buildings are scarce. Since renovation is less costly, this approach is being used to update facilities.

The first such renovations were to three original "pillbox" buildings: Grant Hall, Lincoln Hall, and Douglas Hall.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-44) The renovated buildings use solar and geothermal power which required digging fifty wells 500 feet into the ground east of University Hall. The energy savings of 20–25% led to Lincoln Hall and Douglas Hall being certified US [LEED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design "Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design") Gold. Grant Hall did not apply for LEED certification even though it was the prototype for many of the features found on Lincoln and Douglas Halls.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Lincoln_Hall_sustainability-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Grant_Hall_sustainability-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Douglas_Hall_latest-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-Douglas_Hall_sustainability-48) The new fascia are all glass and the buildings contain facilities for faculty and students. There are plans to expand the renovation project to every lecture hall cluster if the pilot program is successful.

Other campus renovations include the roof of the Behavioral Sciences Building and the terrace of the Education, Performing Arts, and Social Work building.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-49) A brand new building housing the College of Engineering was opened in 2019 to accommodate the increased enrollment in the college. It features the only [high bay structural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_bay_warehouse "High bay warehouse") laboratory in the city of Chicago.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-50)

To accommodate the rising enrollment in the computer science department, a new building is being constructed called the Computer Design Research and Learning Center (CDRLC); it is slated to be completed in the fall of 2024, with a budget of $117.8 million.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-51)
