## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [UIC Flames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC_Flames "UIC Flames")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/UIC_pavilion_%28Chicago%2C_USA%29.JPG/250px-UIC_pavilion_%28Chicago%2C_USA%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UIC_pavilion_(Chicago,_USA).JPG)

[Credit Union 1 Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Union_1_Arena "Credit Union 1 Arena")

The Illinois–Chicago (UIC) athletic teams are called the Flames, a reference to the [1871 Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_Great_Chicago_Fire "1871 Great Chicago Fire"). The university is a member of the [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") level of the [National Collegiate Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA), primarily competing in the [Missouri Valley Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Valley_Conference "Missouri Valley Conference") (MVC) since the 2022–23 academic year.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-89) The Flames previously competed in the D-I [Horizon League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizon_League "Horizon League") from 1994–95 to 2021–22; in the D-I [Mid-Continent Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_League "Summit League") (Mid-Con, now currently known as the Summit League since the 2007–08 school year) from 1982–83 to 1993–94; as an [NCAA D-I Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_independent_schools "NCAA Division I independent schools") during the 1981–82 school year; and in the [Chicagoland Collegiate Athletic Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicagoland_Collegiate_Athletic_Conference "Chicagoland Collegiate Athletic Conference") (CCAC) of the [National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Intercollegiate_Athletics "National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics") (NAIA) from 1949–50 to about 1980–81.

UIC competes in 18 intercollegiate varsity sports:[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago#cite_note-90) Men's sports include baseball, basketball, cross country, soccer, swimming & diving, tennis and track & field (indoor and outdoor); while women's sports include basketball, cross country, golf, soccer, softball, swimming & diving, tennis, track & field (indoor and outdoor) and volleyball.

### Men's soccer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Men's soccer")]

In September 2006, the men's soccer team earned its highest ranking in school history when the SoccerTimes.com College Coaches Poll pegged the Flames at No. 6 in the country. In November 2006, UIC defeated Western Illinois 3–0 in the opening round of the NCAA tournament before falling in the second round to Notre Dame 1–0. UIC finished the 2006 season as the nation's best defensive squad after allowing a mere eight goals in over 1993 minutes of play during 21 matches for a goals-against average (GAA) of 0.36. The GAA was tops in the nation in 2006 and it also ranked fifth all-time in NCAA history. UIC posted 13 shutouts and never allowed more than a single goal in a match. UIC also allowed just two goals after intermission the entire season. Along with the GAA mark, UIC posted the nation's best save percentage with a 0.908 rate.

In 2007, UIC soccer's successful season culminated in an Elite-Eight appearance in the NCAA tournament by way of wins over No. 12 St. Louis, Northwestern, and No. 8 Creighton. In a bid for a Final-Four appearance, UIC fell to Massachusetts 2–1. At season's end, UIC had a record of 13–6–6 and was named a top 10 team by the [National Soccer Coaches Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Soccer_Coaches "United Soccer Coaches") (NSCAA).

### Baseball

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Baseball")]

UIC's baseball team recorded 30 or more victories in a nine-year stretch from 2001 to 2010, won seven straight Horizon League Championships, and advanced to an NCAA regional four times (2003, 2005, 2007, 2008). UIC baseball has recorded regional wins against No. 1 Long Beach State in 2007 and No. 2 Dallas Baptist University in 2008.

### Gymnastics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Gymnastics")]

In 1978 and 1979 the UIC men's gymnastics team won the school's only NCAA team titles at the Division II Championships. Following the 1979 season the men's gymnastics program entered Division I competition and finished the season ranked 10th, Nationally. After the successful 1980 season the remainder of the UIC athletic teams ascended to Division I status. The 1996 men's gymnastics team finished the season in 9th place, the school's highest final ranking among all sports. UIC Men's Gymnastics individual Division I All America honorees include: Paul Fina (Rings), Mike Costa (Pommel Horse, twice), Barry McDonald (Parallel Bars), Shannon Welker (Floor Exercise), Neil Faustino (Vault), and Andrew Stover (Horizontal Bar).

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. # We Help Graduate Students 

Find Housing…**Without the Hassle**

![Image 3: Screen Shot 2020-02-11 at 8.40.08 AM (1).png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5dcdc260265e4c3537eac275/1581435693736-6MHQC5RQPWGBYXJ9AZ0U/Screen+Shot+2020-02-11+at+8.40.08+AM+%281%29.png)

Contact StudentSpace

This is the first and most important step. Beyond finding you the perfect apartment, we are here to be your consultant on every step from targeting the right neighborhood to setting up utilities and everything in between. We are accessible via phone, email, text, facetime, skype, etc.

[Get Started](https://www.student-space.com/find-your-space)

![Image 5](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5dcdc260265e4c3537eac275/1575415820647-TSMGLF0OZ8ZBGYSU9DUT/image-asset.jpeg)

Evaluate All Your Options

With hundreds of online scams and unreliable listings, navigating the rental marketplace is a challenge. That’s why we work closely with you to narrow down your options, and your school loves that we only work with reputable landlords so you know you’re getting the best quality.

[Get Started](https://www.student-space.com/find-your-space)

![Image 6](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5dcdc260265e4c3537eac275/1575413770679-KMD38U2S43KOS3SCUETY/image-asset.jpeg)

Set Up a Tour

We work with your schedule so you can visit your top choices and make the most of your trip. We drive you around to all the showings. Unable to visit prior to your move-in date? Not a problem – We will help you sign a lease remotely.

[Get Started](https://www.student-space.com/find-your-space)

![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5dcdc260265e4c3537eac275/1575413880180-8JP4Q2E4BZNDFJEQJPWT/image-asset.jpeg)

Sign A Lease

The service doesn’t stop once you’ve signed a lease. We are here to answer any questions during and after your move-in, whether you need help with renter’s insurance, furnishing your apartment or even finding the best places to eat nearby.

[Get Started](https://www.student-space.com/find-your-space)

Testimonials

[](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/nntz7h4dgzqurcf4say44af4v4ha78)

## “I´m an exchange student at Northwestern University, and Tyler helped me find a perfect short term rental remotely. He was extremely helpful and kind and responded to all my questions. Tyler, thank you again for your help! I ended up in a great place, with a great location and according to my budget.”

Jorgelina Maria Navar – NU Law

[Read more →](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/nntz7h4dgzqurcf4say44af4v4ha78)

[](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/faedw5z6r3owsi6d8c870ua027xbz2)

## “I am a parent of a student at Northwestern University and needed assistance finding affordable housing for my son. Tyler Roth provided us with excellent service! He was friendly and very easy to work with given our short time frame. He found an affordable and safe place for us. We were very happy to have Tyler’s assistance and knowledge of the area. I would highly recommend him to anyone in need of housing at the University!”

Kim – NU Feinberg

[Read more →](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/faedw5z6r3owsi6d8c870ua027xbz2)

[](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/ut01zdyjvyaugkrv0ryfpied9xj4do)

## “Tyler Roth at StudentSpace gave me tremendous support and assistance finding the right apartment for me in Chicago. Tyler fully understood my needs and was very responsive and helpful. My husband and I are very happy with our choice, and I wouldn’t have been able to spot this satisfying apartment if it weren’t for Tyler's help and advice.”

-Jimin Choi – NU Law

[Read more →](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/ut01zdyjvyaugkrv0ryfpied9xj4do)

[](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/pd4idsxl0aun6qmpt43b6dsuhfdvfj)

## “I’ve just moved from Tokyo to Chicago and just wanted to say thanks for providing StudentSpace as a service. As an international student, navigating the real estate market in Chicago remotely on my own would have been a nightmare and Tyler has been a tremendous help throughout the process. Thanks”

Lui – UC Booth

[Read more →](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/pd4idsxl0aun6qmpt43b6dsuhfdvfj)

[](https://www.student-space.com/testimonials-blog/dyi7sn3bl33wdxypmiig55oeqfq9ch)

## “The StudentSpace service was amazing! Tyler quickly connected me with leasing agents and I was able to find an apartment within 2 weeks in my price range that matched all of my requests. I did this all remotely and highly recommend this service!”

Anouk – Northwestern University

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. The University may also allow third parties to place Cookies on your device that collect and use anonymous information about your visits to, and interactions with, our websites to personalize advertisements and promotional materials for University goods and services. Targeting Cookies may be used by our third-party contractors or our advertising partners to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other sites. We may share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising, and analytics partners who may combine it with other information that you have provided to them or that they have collected from your use of their services. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you will still see advertisements, but they will be less targeted to your interests.

July 15, 2026

In June, the Justice Department opened new investigations into potential race discrimination in admissions at 15 unnamed medical schools.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/04/joseph-karl-grant-appointed-dean-of-the-north-carolina-central-university-school-of-law/ "Joseph Karl Grant Appointed Dean of the North Carolina Central University School of Law")

### [Joseph Karl Grant Appointed Dean of the North Carolina Central University School of Law](https://jbhe.com/2026/04/joseph-karl-grant-appointed-dean-of-the-north-carolina-central-university-school-of-law/ "Joseph Karl Grant Appointed Dean of the North Carolina Central University School of Law")

April 13, 2026

Professor Grant comes to North Carolina Central University from Capital University in Columbus, Ohio, where he most recently served as interim dean and the Josiah H. Blackmore II/Shirley M. Nault Chair in Legal Education in the School of Law.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/04/how-do-professional-schools-at-hbcus-fare-in-us-news-rankings/ "How Do Professional Schools at HBCUs Fare in *U.S. News* Rankings?")

### [How Do Professional Schools at HBCUs Fare in *U.S. News* Rankings?](https://jbhe.com/2026/04/how-do-professional-schools-at-hbcus-fare-in-us-news-rankings/ "How Do Professional Schools at HBCUs Fare in *U.S. News* Rankings?")

April 8, 2026

Some of the graduate and professional schools at historically Black colleges and universities were included in the _U.S. News_ rankings, but in all cases, they were far down the list of the best schools and programs.

[](https://jbhe.com/2026/03/how-changes-to-federal-student-loan-programs-could-impact-hbcu-medical-schools-and-students/ "How Changes to Federal Student Loan Programs Could Impact HBCU Medical Schools and Students")

### [How Changes to Federal Student Loan Programs Could Impact HBCU Medical Schools and Students](https://jbhe.com/2026/03/how-changes-to-federal-student-loan-programs-could-impact-hbcu-medical-schools-and-students/ "How Changes to Federal Student Loan Programs Could Impact HBCU Medical Schools and Students")

March 23, 2026

Effective July 1, there will be new annual and aggregate borrowing limits on federal loans used for graduate programs. According to a new analysis from the Century Foundation, these limits are far below the median cost of attending both public and private medical institutions, which suggests many students will need to take on private loans or choose not to attend medical school at all.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

University committed to research as a central part of its mission

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg/250px-Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_(1769-1830)_-_Charles_William,_Baron_von_Humboldt_(1767-1835)_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg)

[Wilhelm von Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_von_Humboldt "Wilhelm von Humboldt"), credited with the [Humboldtian model of higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldtian_model_of_higher_education "Humboldtian model of higher education")

A **research university** or a **research-intensive university** is a [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University "University") that is committed to [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") as a central part of its mission.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Taylor-4) They are "the key sites of [knowledge production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_production_modes "Knowledge production modes")", along with "intergenerational [knowledge transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_transfer "Knowledge transfer") and the certification of new knowledge" through the awarding of [doctoral degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy"), and continue to be "the very center of scientific productivity".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Powell-5) They can be [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university") or [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university"), and often have well-known brand names.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-CollegeSolution-6)

Undergraduate courses at many research universities are often academic rather than [vocational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocational_university "Vocational university") and may not prepare students for particular careers, but many employers value degrees from research universities because they teach fundamental [life skills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_skills "Life skills") such as [critical thinking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_thinking "Critical thinking").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Andreatta2-7) Globally, research universities are overwhelmingly [public institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_universities "Public universities"), while some countries like the United States and Japan also have well-known [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_universities "Private universities") research institutions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)

Institutions of higher education that are not research universities or do not aspire to that designation, such as [liberal arts colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_arts_college "Liberal arts college"), instead place more emphasis on student instruction or other aspects of tertiary education, whereas research university faculty members, in contrast, are under more pressure to [publish or perish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish_or_perish "Publish or perish").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Irons-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th century")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall,_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore,_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif)

[Johns Hopkins University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University") in [Baltimore, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore") (Gilman Hall pictured), founded in 1876, is considered the first research university in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Geiger_Page_8-9)

The concept of the research university first arose in early 19th-century [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia") in Germany, where [Wilhelm von Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_von_Humboldt "Wilhelm von Humboldt") championed his vision of _Einheit von Lehre und Forschung_ (the unity of teaching and research), as a means of producing an education that focused on the main areas of knowledge, including the natural sciences, social sciences, and [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities"), rather than on the previous goals of the university education, which was to develop an understanding of truth, beauty, and [goodness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good "Good").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Menand-11)

The concept was brought to Britain in the mid-19th century by [Henry Enfield Roscoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Roscoe_(chemist) "Henry Roscoe (chemist)"), who had studied with [Robert Wilhelm Bunsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wilhelm_Bunsen "Robert Wilhelm Bunsen") at the [University of Heidelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Heidelberg "University of Heidelberg"). In 1857 he was appointed professor of chemistry at [Owen's College, Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen's_College,_Manchester "Owen's College, Manchester"), and worked during the 1860s to develop the college following the [German model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldtian_model_of_higher_education "Humboldtian model of higher education").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-15) The emphasis on research from the German model was taken up by the other [civic university colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redbrick_universities "Redbrick universities") founded in England in the latter part of the 19th century.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-16) Research schools were founded by individual academics at some institutions from the 1870s, and from the 1890s research was pursued as a matter of institutional policy.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-17) British universities also set up research degrees in this period; however, these were [higher doctorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_doctorate "Higher doctorate"), starting with the [Doctor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Science "Doctor of Science") at Durham in 1882 and Cambridge in 1883, aimed at a higher level than the PhD, or lower degrees such as Oxford's BPhil and BSc, Cambridge's BA by research, and the MA by dissertation at London and other newer universities.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Howarth-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-19)

[Roger L. Geiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Geiger "Roger L. Geiger"), "the leading historian of the American research university,"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Macintyre_Page_333-20) has argued that "the model for the American research university was established by five of the nine [colonial colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_colleges "Colonial colleges") chartered before the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution") ([Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), [Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"), and [King's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University")); five state universities ([Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan"), [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana%E2%80%93Champaign "University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign"), and [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley")); and five private institutions conceived from their inception as research universities ([MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), [Cornell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University"), [Johns Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University"), [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), and [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"))."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Crow-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Geiger_Page_3-22) The American research university first emerged in the late 19th century, when these fifteen institutions began to graft graduate programs derived from the German model onto undergraduate programs derived from the British model.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Crow-21) At Johns Hopkins, president [Daniel Coit Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Coit_Gilman "Daniel Coit Gilman") led the development of the American research university[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Geiger_Page_8-9) by setting high standards for recruiting faculty and admitting students, and insisting that faculty members had to commit to both teaching and research.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Benson_Page_x-23)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Aston_Webb_Hall%2C_Birmingham_University.jpg/250px-Aston_Webb_Hall%2C_Birmingham_University.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aston_Webb_Hall,_Birmingham_University.jpg)

The [University of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham "University of Birmingham"), UK, made vital research contributions during World War Two, including the [Cavity magnetron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavity_magnetron "Cavity magnetron") that made airborne [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") possible and the [Frisch–Peierls memorandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisch%E2%80%93Peierls_memorandum "Frisch–Peierls memorandum") that first demonstrated that an [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") was technically feasible.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-24)

In the early 20th century, the tension between research-led teaching after Humboldt's model in the English civic university colleges and the centrally set examinations of the [Victoria University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_University_(UK) "Victoria University (UK)") and the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") was one of the factors that contributed to the university colleges becoming universities in their own right.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-25)

Research universities were essential to the establishment of American [hegemony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemony "Hegemony") by the end of the 20th century.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Marginson_Page_67-26) Columbia and Harvard were instrumental in the early development of the [American film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") in Hollywood in the first half of the 20th century.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Decherney-27)

The first [Congress of Universities of the (British) Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Commonwealth_Universities "Association of Commonwealth Universities") in 1912 was urged by the Foreign Office to adopt the PhD in order to prevent students going to study in Germany and America. However, this was opposed at that time as diluting the standard of English doctorates. In 1917, a conference of the universities of Birmingham, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield decided to introduce the PhD, and this was followed by all British universities except Cambridge, which maintained its BA by research into the 1920s.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Howarth-18)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-28)

The development of [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons "Nuclear weapons") in the 1940s, culminating in the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project"), involved researchers from universities in the US (Berkeley, Chicago, Columbia, and Princeton) and the UK (Birmingham and Cambridge).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Reed_Page_122-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-30)

MIT and Stanford were leaders in building the American [military–industrial complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military%E2%80%93industrial_complex "Military–industrial complex") in the aftermath of World War II.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-31) and developing [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Boden_Page_734-32)

The first electronic [stored-program computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stored-program_computer "Stored-program computer"), the [Manchester Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Baby "Manchester Baby"), was developed at Manchester in the 1940s,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-33) while in the US Berkeley and Stanford played a central role in the development of [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-34) The "most prestigious group of research universities" in the United States is the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Smith_Page_78-35)

In the second half of the 20th century, American research universities became the model for research universities around the world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach-2)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Graham-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Vest_Page_7-37) Having one or more universities based on the American model (including the use of [English as a lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_as_a_lingua_franca "English as a lingua franca")) thus became a marker of "social progress and [modernity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity")" for countries.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Stevens_Page_129-38)

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 21st century")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Research_spending_gdp%2C_World%2C_2023_%28cropped%29.svg/500px-Research_spending_gdp%2C_World%2C_2023_%28cropped%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Research_spending_gdp,_World,_2023_(cropped).svg)

Research spending as a share of GDP by country

By the early 21st century it had become difficult for European universities to maintain research standards and resources at the level of the top US institutions.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Wittrock-39)

[Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar") and the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") (UAE) funded research universities to establish [international branch campuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_branch_campus "International branch campus") in those countries, and they and other Gulf states also started to build up their own research universities, such as [Khalifa University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalifa_University "Khalifa University") (UAE), [Hamad Bin Khalifa University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamad_Bin_Khalifa_University "Hamad Bin Khalifa University") (Qatar) and [KAUST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KAUST "KAUST") (Saudi Arabia), by recruiting Western-trained faculty and staff. By 2023, Qatar and the UAE had passed the US in number of papers published per 1000 population, although still behind Britain, Sweden and Singapore.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Economist-40) As of April 2026, the UAE hosted 39 branch campuses, behind only China, with twelve institutions from the UK, seven from India, and three each from Australia, France, Russia and the US, while Qatar hosted twelve branch campuses, the majority from US institutions.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-41) The amount of funding given to US universities by Qatar led to concerns about [Qatari involvement in US higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatari_involvement_in_US_higher_education "Qatari involvement in US higher education").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-42)

[Academic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_freedom "Academic freedom") – identified by Altbach as one of the key characteristics of successful research universities[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach2013-43) – declined globally from 2012, as measured by the _Academic Freedom Index_. The trend started in Latin America, the Middle East, Asia and North Africa, but spread to established liberal democracies. The US, in particular, saw a decline from 2020. [Jeremy Berg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_M._Berg "Jeremy M. Berg") noted that the dependence of research universities in the US on federal research funding gave the government leverage to override international autonomy, and that while some universities, such as Harvard, had pushed back and won in court, many had not.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-44)

## Characteristics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Characteristics")]

John Taylor, Professor of Higher Education Management at the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool"), defines the key characteristics of successful research universities as:[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Taylor-4)

*   "Presence of pure and applied research"
*   "Delivery of research-led teaching"
*   "Breadth of [academic disciplines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_discipline "Academic discipline")"
*   "High proportion of [postgraduate research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postgraduate_research "Postgraduate research") programmes"
*   "High levels of external income"
*   "An international perspective"

Philip Altbach defines a different, although similar, set of key characteristics for what research universities need to become successful:[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach2013-43)

*   At the top of the academic hierarchy in a differentiated higher education system and receiving appropriate support
*   Overwhelmingly [public institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")
*   Little competition from non-university research institutions, unless these have strong connections to the universities
*   More funding than other universities to attract the best staff and students and support research infrastructure
*   Adequate and sustained budgets
*   Potential for income generation from student fees and intellectual property
*   Suitable facilities
*   Autonomy
*   [Academic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_freedom "Academic freedom")

A 2012 [National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academies_of_Sciences,_Engineering,_and_Medicine "National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine") report defined research universities, in the American context, as having values of intellectual freedom, initiative and creativity, excellence, and openness, with such additional characteristics as:[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-45)

*   Being large and comprehensive – [Clark Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Kerr "Clark Kerr")'s "multiversity"
*   Emphasizing the undergraduate residential experience (flagged specifically as distinguishing American research universities from those in continental Europe)
*   Integrating [graduate education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postgraduate_education "Postgraduate education") with research
*   Having faculty engaged in research and scholarship
*   Conducting research at high levels
*   Having enlightened and bold leadership

Global [university rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_and_university_rankings#Global_rankings "College and university rankings") use metrics that primarily measure research to rank universities.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-IHE_2010-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-HEPI-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-48) Some also have criteria for inclusion based on the concept of a research university such as teaching at both undergraduate and postgraduate level and conducting work in multiple faculties (_[QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS\_World\_University\_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")_),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-49) or teaching undergraduates, having a research output of more than 1,000 research papers over 5 years, and no more than 80% of activity in a single subject area (_[Times Higher Education World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times\_Higher\_Education\_World\_University\_Rankings "Times Higher Education World University Rankings"))_.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-50)

The [Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") in the United States designates institutions that spend on average at least $2.5 million on research and development annually as 'research universities and colleges', with further designations of 'research 2: high spending and doctorate production' and 'research 1: very high spending and doctorate production' for institutions spending over $5 million and awarding 20 or more doctorates per year and institutions spending over $50 million and awarding 70 or more doctorates per year respectively.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-51)As of 2025,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit) there were 187 R1 universities, 139 R2 universities and 216 other research universities in the US out of 3,941 total institutions classified.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-52)

## Worldwide distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Worldwide distribution")]

The _[QS World University Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS\_World\_University\_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")_ for 2021 included 1,002 research universities. The region with the highest number was [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"), with 39.8%, followed by [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")/Pacific with 26.7%, the [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") with 15.6%, [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") with 10.8%, and the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East") and [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") with 7%. All regions except the Middle East and Africa were represented in the top 100. The largest number of new entrants to the rankings were from [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") and [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe"), followed by [Southern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Europe "Southern Europe").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-53) By individual country, the US had the most institutions with 151, followed by the UK with 84, China with 51 and Germany with 45. The top 200 showed a similar pattern with the US having 45 universities, the UK 26 and Germany 12.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-54) By comparison, the [Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") (2015) identified 115 US universities as "Doctoral Universities: Highest Research Activity" and a further 107 as "Doctoral Universities: Higher Research Activity", while Altbach estimated that there were around 220 research universities in the US in 2013.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-55)

The _[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic\_Ranking\_of\_World\_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")_ for 2020 showed a similar distribution, with 185 of their 500 ranked institutions coming from Europe, 161 from the Americas, 149 from Asia/Oceania and five from Africa. All regions except Africa were represented in the top 100, although the Americas were represented solely by universities from the United States and Canada.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-56) In 2026, China had the most universities in the top 500, 125, followed by the US with 111, the UK with 35 and Germany with 35.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-57) However, the top 200 shows the different pattern: the US with 59 followed by China with 40 and the UK with 17.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-58)

The 2027 _[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times\_Higher\_Education\_World\_University\_Rankings "Times Higher Education World University Rankings")_ only gave a breakdown by country and only for its top 200; this again had the US at the top with 53, followed by the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") with 25, [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") with 19 and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") with 17. The top 200 featured one university from Africa, the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town") in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), and one university from Latin America, the [University of São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo "University of São Paulo") in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-59) The _[U.S. News & World Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.\_News\_&\_World\_Report "U.S. News & World Report")_ Best Global Universities Ranking 2026 gave numbers by country for the 2250 universities ranked from more than 100 countries: China was the top, with 409, followed by the US with 275 and India with 123.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-60) However, the U.S. had 113 schools in the top 500, followed by China with 71 schools and the UK with 40.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-61) The 2025 _[CWTS Leiden Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CWTS\_Leiden\_Ranking "CWTS Leiden Ranking")_ included 1,594 universities in the rankings from 77 countries/regions: China topped the list, with 356, followed by the US with 204 and the UK with 61.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-62)

## THREE UNIVERSITIES.

 ONE SYSTEM.

 ALTOGETHER EXTRAORDINARY.

**Fueled by countless supporters and driven by the most talented individuals, we explore further, dive deeper, and reach higher.** When you radically rethink potential, the impossible is made possible every day—in a thriving, micro-urban community; in the heart of a big city; and in the state capital. Combined, our three universities and healthcare enterprise bring resources, capabilities, and drive that are greater than the sum of their parts—it is altogether extraordinary.

## ACCESS FOR UNDERREPRESENTED STUDENTS AT AN ALL-TIME HIGH

**Our efforts to provide access to more students across the state are producing results, including increasing the number of underrepresented students.** In the fall of 2025, underrepresented students made up 33 percent of all undergraduate students in the U of I System, an all-time high.

[EXPLORE ENROLLMENT DATA](https://uillinois.edu/data/enrollment)

## EXTRAORDINARY REACH

**From Rockford to Chicago to the Quad Cities, Peoria and the southern tip of Illinois, the University of Illinois System touches virtually every field, forest and city block in our state.** In fact, more than half of all students enrolled in a public university in Illinois are enrolled at one of our three universities. We have students from 101 of 102 Illinois counties, and 79 percent of our undergraduates are in-state students.

![Image 9: 53% all of Illinois public university attendees go to University of Illinois System schools](https://uillinois.edu/userfiles/servers/server_1240/image/extraordinary_reach_graph_2025.svg)

We have students from 101 of 102 Illinois counties![Image 10](https://uillinois.edu/userfiles/servers/server_1240/image/datastories/system/impact_map_simplified_2021.svg)

## FINANCIAL AID

**Our commitment to access provides the opportunity to obtain a life-changing education to more students than ever.** To make that possible, nearly half the aid our undergraduate students received – $298 million in Fiscal Year 2024 – comes from our universities. Over the past 10 years, those expenditures increased by nearly 50%. Sixty percent of our undergraduates pay less than full tuition and fees, and 33% pay nothing at all.

## University of Illinois - Cookie Information

### About Cookies

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. The University may also allow third parties to place Cookies on your device that collect and use anonymous information about your visits to, and interactions with, our websites to personalize advertisements and promotional materials for University goods and services. Targeting Cookies may be used by our third-party contractors or our advertising partners to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other sites. We may share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising, and analytics partners who may combine it with other information that you have provided to them or that they have collected from your use of their services. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you will still see advertisements, but they will be less targeted to your interests.

Cookies and related technologies (herein “Cookies”) are small text files that a website saves on your computer when you visit the site. Cookies the University sets are called first-party Cookies. The data collected might be about you, your device, your preferences, or your login information. This data is mostly used to make the website work as expected so, for example, you don’t have to keep re-entering your credentials whenever you come back to the site. Cookies set by third parties are called third-party Cookies. We use third-party Cookies for analyzing website traffic and our advertising and marketing efforts. We have divided the Cookies we use into the following categories: Strictly Necessary, Performance, Functional, and Targeting. Under each category heading below you will find a general description of the Cookies in each category. You can change your browser settings to block, delete, or alert you to Cookies. The Help menu on the menu bar of most browsers will tell you how to do that. However, if you do, you may have to manually adjust preferences every time you visit a site and some features may not work as intended.

See the [**University of Illinois System Cookie Policy**Link opens in a new window](https://www.vpaa.uillinois.edu/resources/cookies) for more information.

 Strictly Necessary Cookies - Always Active 
Strictly Necessary Cookies are first-party Cookies that are necessary for the website to function. They can be either permanent or temporary and are usually only set in response to actions made directly by you that amount to a request for services, such as logging in or filling in forms. For example, we use Strictly Necessary Cookies to handle user registration and login. Some sites require the use of Strictly Necessary Cookies to access the site, such as University websites requiring University credentialed authentication. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, you may not be able to access the site or some parts of the site will not work.

 Performance Cookies - Always Active 
Performance Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance and effectiveness of University websites. Performance Cookies also help the University understand which webpages are the most and least popular, see how visitors move around the site, and determine whether webpage content is relevant to user interests. Performance Cookies may be first-party or third party, permanent or temporary, and do not personally identify individual visitors. Some Performance Cookies are “analytics” Cookies (e.g., Google Analytics), using third-party software tools, which help us understand more about how our websites are used and where visitors come from by collecting and aggregating anonymous information on the pages visited and any advertisements viewed. The University does not take responsibility for the collection, use, and management of data by any third-party software tool provider unless required to do so by applicable law. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some site services and functionalities may not work.

 Functional Cookies - Always Active 
Functional Cookies enhance the performance and functionality of our websites but are non-essential to their use. These permanent Cookies allow our website to remember information from your previous visits, such as details you submitted before or your previously stated preferences. These Cookies may also be used to provide services you request, such as newsletters or publications. They may be first- or third-party Cookies that enable services we have added to our webpages. If you set your browser to block or delete Cookies, some or all of these services may not function properly.

 Targeting Cookies - Always Active 
Targeting Cookies are used to deliver content tailored to your interests and may be temporary or permanent. They may also be first-party or third-party Cookies. Targeting Cookies are based on uniquely identifying your browser and device; they do not store information such as your name. The University may use targeting Cookies prepared by the University, its third-party contractors, or advertising partners to provide you with personalized University display advertising and promotional material about the University and its programs. The University may also allow third parties to place Cookies on your device that collect and use anonymous information about your visits to, and interactions with, our websites to personalize advertisements and promotional materials for University goods and services. Targeting Cookies may be used by our third-party contractors or our advertising partners to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other sites. We may share information about your use of our site

# Professional Schools

[](link_11)

### [Medical Schools Face Further Scrutiny on Their Admissions Policies](link_11)

July 15, 2026

In June, the Justice Department opened new investigations into potential race discrimination in admissions at 15 unnamed medical schools.

[](link_12)

### [Joseph Karl Grant Appointed Dean of the North Carolina Central University School of Law](link_12)

April 13, 2026

Professor Grant comes to North Carolina Central University from Capital University in Columbus, Ohio, where he most recently served as interim dean and the Josiah H. Blackmore II/Shirley M. Nault Chair in Legal Education in the School of Law.

[](link_13)

### [How Do Professional Schools at HBCUs Fare in *U.S. News* Rankings?](link_13)

April 8, 2026

Some of the graduate and professional schools at historically Black colleges and universities were included in the _U.S. News_ rankings, but in all cases, they were far down the list of the best schools and programs.

[](link_14)

### [How Changes to Federal Student Loan Programs Could Impact HBCU Medical Schools and Students](link_14)

March 23, 2026

Effective July 1, there will be new annual and aggregate borrowing limits on federal loans used for graduate programs. According to a new analysis from the Century Foundation, these limits are far below the median cost of attending both public and private medical institutions, which suggests many students will need to take on private loans or choose not to attend medical school at all.

[](link_15)

### [Higher Education Gifts or Grants of Interest to African Americans](link_15)

February 18, 2026

Here is this week’s news of grants or gifts to historically Black colleges and universities or for programs of particular interest to African Americans in higher education.

[](link_16)

### [Danielle M. Conway Is the New President of the Association of American Law Schools](link_16)

January 19, 2026

“This is a pivotal moment for us all in the legal academy to come together in coalition around academic freedom,” said Professor Conway, dean of Penn State Dickinson Law and the School of International Affairs. “We may disagree on many other things, but we must collectively uphold academic freedom.”

[](link_17)

### [More Black Students Applied, but Fewer Were Accepted to U.S. Medical Schools in 2025](link_17)

December 22, 2025

For the 2025-2026 academic year, Black students represented 11.3 percent of all applicants, but only 8.4 percent of all matriculants to medical schools in the United States. This is a significant decline from 2021-2022, when Black students' representation among medical school matriculants peaked at 11.7 percent.

[](link_18)

### [Howard University Launches New Doctorate in Interdisciplinary Biomedical Sciences](link_18)

October 17, 2025

“This program opens new pathways for discovery, equity, and leadership in medicine and research,” said Dana Williams, dean of the Howard University Graduate School. “The cross-disciplinary work of our students will shape the next generation of physician-scientists and biomedical innovators.”

[](link_19)

### [Charles R. Drew University Establishes New Partnership With American University of Antigua](link_19)

October 10, 2025

Through this new partnership, eligible Charles R. Drew University students are guaranteed admission into the medical degree program at American University of Antigua College of Medicine.

[](link_20)

### [Penn Law School Launches New Fellowship Named for Its First Black Woman Graduate](link_20)

October 7, 2025

The new fellowship follows the recent closure of Penn Carey Law's Office of Equal Opportunity and Engagement and a pause in the Sadie T. M. Alexander Scholarship program, which covered tuition for students who planned to focus their studies and future law practice on racial justice.

[](link_21)

### [A Pair of New Deans at Historically Black Universities](link_21)

October 6, 2025

Ofosuwa M. Abiola is dean of the Graduate School at Bowie State University in Maryland and Vonda M. Easterling is dean of students at Fort Valley State University in Georgia.

[](link_22)

### [LSU Announces Resignation of Law School Dean, But She Claims Discrimination](link_22)

September 22, 2025

Alena Allen, the first Black law school dean at Louisiana State University, claims the university has discriminated against her, forcing her to resign from her position after she raised concerns about the school's finances.

[](link_23)

### [Vanderbilt University Partners With Tennessee State University for Sports Medicine Training](link_23)

September 19, 2025

The new agreement will provide Tennessee State University students studying human performance and sports science with hands-on training opportunities in athletic training and sports medicine at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

[](link_24)

### [New Partnership Creates Pathway to Careers in Podiatric Medicine for Charles R. Drew University Students](link_24)

September 17, 2025

Through a new partnership with Western University of Health Sciences, students at historically Black Charles R. Drew University of Medicine and Science in Los Angeles now have access to a streamlined admissions process into WesternU's doctor of podiatric medicine degree program.

[](link_25)

### [Charles R. Drew University Establishes New Partnership With the University of California, Riverside](link_25)

May 30, 2025

The partnership will connect faculty and staff at Charles R. Drew University with students who are members of several Identity Centers at the University of California, Riverside. Participating students will be introduced to CDU's graduate and professional programs and special priority for scholarship opportunities will be provided to UCR students who choose to enroll at the historically Black medical school.

[](link_26)

### [Texas Southern University Requests $120 Million to Construct New Building for Its Law School](link_26)

March 21, 2025

In 2021, the American Bar Association informed Texas Southern University that the HBCU's law school building did not comply with safety standards, putting the law school at risk of losing accreditation. To make the required updates, the university has recently requested $120 million from state legislators.

[](link_27)

### [Partnership Provides Tennessee State University Students With Accelerated Pathway to Medical School](link_27)

March 14, 2025

Tennessee State University undergraduate students now have the opportunity to earn a bachelor's degree in biology and chemistry from TSU and a medical degree at Belmont University in just seven years, reducing the traditional timeline for a medical doctorate by one year.

[](link_28)

### [Morehouse School of Medicine Establishes Partnership With a Local Healthcare System](link_28)

March 7, 2025

Morehouse School of Medicine has recently partnered with Phoebe Putney Health System to create new residency programs, develop clinical training opportunities for students, expand the physician pipeline, and address local health needs.

[](link_29)

### [Kenneth Chance to Step Down as Dean of Case Western Reserve University Dental School](link_29)

March 5, 2025

Dr. Chance was appointed dean of the Case Western Reserve University School of Dental Medicine in 2014, making him the school's first Black dean.

[](link_30)

### [Alvin Washington Appointed Chancellor of the Southern University Law Center](link_30)

March 3, 2025

Professor Washington has been a faculty member with Southern University Law Center for over two decades. He is an expert in conflict resolution and has mediated hundreds of cases at the federal, state, and local level.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

University committed to research as a central part of its mission

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg/250px-Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_%281769-1830%29_-_Charles_William%2C_Baron_von_Humboldt_%281767-1835%29_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sir_Thomas_Lawrence_(1769-1830)_-_Charles_William,_Baron_von_Humboldt_(1767-1835)_-_RCIN_404936_-_Royal_Collection.jpg)

[Wilhelm von Humboldt](link_3), credited with the [Humboldtian model of higher education](link_4)

A **research university** or a **research-intensive university** is a [university](link_5) that is committed to [research](link_0) as a central part of its mission.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Altbach-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Taylor-4) They are "the key sites of [knowledge production](link_6)", along with "intergenerational [knowledge transfer](link_7) and the certification of new knowledge" through the awarding of [doctoral degrees](link_8), and continue to be "the very center of scientific productivity".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Powell-5) They can be [public](link_9) or [private](link_10), and often have well-known brand names.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-CollegeSolution-6)

Undergraduate courses at many research universities are often academic rather than [vocational](link_11) and may not prepare students for particular careers, but many employers value degrees from research universities because they teach fundamental [life skills](link_12) such as [critical thinking](link_13).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Andreatta2-7) Globally, research universities are overwhelmingly [public institutions](link_14), while some countries like the United States and Japan also have well-known [private](link_15) research institutions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Role-1)

Institutions of higher education that are not research universities or do not aspire to that designation, such as [liberal arts colleges](link_16), instead place more emphasis on student instruction or other aspects of tertiary education, whereas research university faculty members, in contrast, are under more pressure to [publish or perish](link_17).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Irons-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Research_university&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th century")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall%2C_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore%2C_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Interior_of_the_Hutzler_Reading_room_located_in_Gilman_Hall,_on_the_Johns_Hopkins_University_campus_in_Baltimore,_Maryland_LCCN2013646484.tif)

[Johns Hopkins University](link_18) in [Baltimore, Maryland](link_19) (Gilman Hall pictured), founded in 1876, is considered the first research university in the [United States](link_20)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Geiger_Page_8-9)

The concept of the research university first arose in early 19th-century [Prussia](link_21) in Germany, where [Wilhelm von Humboldt](link_3) championed his vision of _Einheit von Lehre und Forschung_ (the unity of teaching and research), as a means of producing an education that focused on the main areas of knowledge, including the natural sciences, social sciences, and [humanities](link_22), rather than on the previous goals of the university education, which was to develop an understanding of truth, beauty, and [goodness](link_23).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university#cite_note-Menand-11)

The concept was brought to Britain in the mid-19th century by [Henry Enfield Roscoe](link_24), who had studied with [Robert Wilhelm Bunsen](link_25) at the [University of Heidelberg](link_26).
