## Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Research")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Dairy_farm_4390.jpg/250px-Dairy_farm_4390.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dairy_farm_4390.jpg)

[Round barns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_barns_in_Illinois "Round barns in Illinois") on the [University of Illinois Experimental Dairy Farm Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Experimental_Dairy_Farm_Historic_District "University of Illinois Experimental Dairy Farm Historic District"), part of [ACES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIUC_College_of_Agriculture,_Consumer,_and_Environmental_Sciences "UIUC College of Agriculture, Consumer, and Environmental Sciences")

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is often regarded as a world-leading magnet for engineering and sciences (both applied and basic).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-95) According to the [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), the university spent $625 million on research and development in 2018, ranking it 37th in the nation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-2018_R&D-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-research.illinois.edu-11) It is also listed as one of the top 25 American research universities by [The Center for Measuring University Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Center_for_Measuring_University_Performance "The Center for Measuring University Performance").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-96)

Besides the annual influx of grants and sponsored projects, the university manages an extensive modern research infrastructure.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-97) The university has been a leader in computer-based education and hosted the [PLATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLATO_(computer_system) "PLATO (computer system)") project, which was a precursor to the internet and resulted in the development of the [plasma display](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_display "Plasma display"). Illinois was a 2nd-generation [ARPAnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPAnet "ARPAnet") site in 1971 and was the first institution to license the [UNIX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNIX "UNIX") operating system from Bell Labs. In [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates")' 2004 talk as part of his five-university campus tour titled "Software Breakthroughs: Solving the Toughest Problems in Computer Science,"[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-98) he mentioned that [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") hired more graduates from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign than from any other university in the world.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-99)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Centers and institutes")]

Main articles: [National Center for Supercomputing Applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Center_for_Supercomputing_Applications "National Center for Supercomputing Applications"), [Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckman_Institute_for_Advanced_Science_and_Technology "Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology"), [Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_R._Woese_Institute_for_Genomic_Biology "Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology"), and [Prairie Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_Research_Institute "Prairie Research Institute")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/BeckmanInstitute.jpg/250px-BeckmanInstitute.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BeckmanInstitute.jpg)

The [Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckman_Institute_for_Advanced_Science_and_Technology "Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology") is the largest interdisciplinary facility on campus, at 313,000 square feet (29,100 m 2).

The university hosts the [National Center for Supercomputing Applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Center_for_Supercomputing_Applications "National Center for Supercomputing Applications") (NCSA), which created [Mosaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_(web_browser) "Mosaic (web browser)"), the first graphical [web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser"), the [Apache HTTP server](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_HTTP_server "Apache HTTP server"), and [NCSA Telnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCSA_Telnet "NCSA Telnet"). The Parallel@Illinois program hosts several programs in [parallel computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing"), including the [Universal Parallel Computing Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UPCRC_Illinois "UPCRC Illinois"). The university contracted with [Cray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cray "Cray") to build the [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation")-funded supercomputer [Blue Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Waters "Blue Waters").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-102) The system also has the largest public online storage system in the world with more than 25 petabytes of usable space.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-103) The university celebrated January 12, 1997, as the "birthday" of [HAL 9000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL_9000 "HAL 9000"), the fictional supercomputer from the novel and film _2001: A Space Odyssey_; in both works, HAL credits "Urbana, Illinois" as his place of operational origin.

The [Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckman_Institute_for_Advanced_Science_and_Technology "Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology") supports interdisciplinary collaborative research in the broad areas of intelligent systems, neuroscience, molecular science and engineering, and biomedical imaging.

The [Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_R._Woese_Institute_for_Genomic_Biology "Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology") supports research in genomics and related areas of biology.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/UofIPrarieResearch.JPG/250px-UofIPrarieResearch.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UofIPrarieResearch.JPG)

One of the university's research [prairie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie "Prairie") fields, located off Florida Avenue

The [Prairie Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_Research_Institute "Prairie Research Institute") on campus houses several divisions, including the [Illinois Natural History Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Natural_History_Survey "Illinois Natural History Survey"), Illinois State Geological Survey, Illinois State Water Survey, Illinois Sustainable Technology Center, and Illinois State Archaeological Survey. Researchers focus on areas such as agriculture, biodiversity, climate, public health, emerging pests, energy, mineral resources, pollution mitigation, and water resources. The Illinois Natural History Survey holds extensive collections, including one of North America's largest insect collections. The Illinois State Geological Survey manages the Illinois Geological Samples Library and paleontological collections. The Illinois State Archaeological Survey preserves a large collection of Illinois archaeological artifacts, including those from the [Cahokia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia "Cahokia") Mounds.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-104)

The Technology Entrepreneur Center at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign offers resources for students to develop their entrepreneurial ideas, including classes, competitions, and workshops.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-105) It hosts events including the Cozad New Venture Challenge, Silicon Valley Entrepreneurship Workshop, Illinois I-Corps, and SocialFuse. The Cozad Challenge, held annually since 2000, provides mentorship and workshops on venture creation, with teams competing for funding.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-106) The Silicon Valley Workshop, a week-long event in January, exposes students to startups, technology companies, and entrepreneurial alumni in [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-107) Illinois I-Corps helps National Science Foundation grantees identify valuable product opportunities from academic research through customer discovery and entrepreneurship training.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-109) SocialFuse is a pitching and networking event where students can present ideas and connect with potential teammates.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-110)

The Center for Plasma-Material Interactions was established in 2004 by Professor David N. Ruzic to research the complex behavior between [ions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion "Ion"), [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron"), and [energetic atoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energetic_neutral_atom "Energetic neutral atom") generated in [plasmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_(physics) "Plasma (physics)") and the surfaces of materials. CPMI encompasses [fusion plasmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") in its research.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-113)

In 2007, the university-hosted research [Institute for Condensed Matter Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Condensed_Matter_Theory "Institute for Condensed Matter Theory") (ICMT) was launched, with the director [Paul Goldbart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Goldbart "Paul Goldbart") and the chief scientist [Anthony Leggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Leggett "Anthony Leggett"). ICMT is located at the Engineering Science Building on campus.

### Notable discoveries and innovations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Notable discoveries and innovations")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/GraingerEngineeringLibrary.jpg/250px-GraingerEngineeringLibrary.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GraingerEngineeringLibrary.jpg)

[Grainger Engineering Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Engineering_Library "Grainger Engineering Library")

In the field of natural sciences, the [BCS theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BCS_theory "BCS theory"), a groundbreaking theory of [superconductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity "Superconductivity"), was proposed by [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") in collaboration with [Leon Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Cooper "Leon Cooper") and his doctoral student [John Robert Schrieffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Robert_Schrieffer "John Robert Schrieffer"). Their work earned them the [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") in 1972.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-washpost-117) In the realm of agricultural science, John Laughnan, while a professor, developed [sweet corn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_corn#Genetics "Sweet corn") with higher-than-normal sugar content, a significant advancement in crop science.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-DLLarson-118)

In computer and applied sciences, several notable achievements originated from the University of Illinois. The [ILLIAC I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ILLIAC_I "ILLIAC I"), built in 1952, was the first computer entirely constructed and owned by a U.S. educational institution. It was also used by [Lejaren Hiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lejaren_Hiller "Lejaren Hiller") and [Leonard Issacson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Issacson "Leonard Issacson") to create the _[Illiac Suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illiac\_Suite "Illiac Suite")_, the first known composition written by an electronic computer.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-Baggi-120) The development of [LLVM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LLVM "LLVM"), initially started by [Vikram Adve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikram_Adve "Vikram Adve") and [Chris Lattner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Lattner "Chris Lattner"), is now recognized as a major project in compiler infrastructure.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-121) Another milestone was the development of the [Mosaic web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosaic_(web_browser) "Mosaic (web browser)") at the [National Center for Supercomputing Applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Center_for_Supercomputing_Applications "National Center for Supercomputing Applications") in 1993.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-mosaic_and_th_w3-122)

[NAMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAMD "NAMD"), a molecular dynamics simulation code, was pioneered by [Klaus Schulten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaus_Schulten "Klaus Schulten") and his team at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, further advancing computational biophysics. The [PLATO system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLATO_(computer_system) "PLATO (computer system)"), also developed at the University of Illinois, was the first generalized [computer assisted instruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_assisted_instruction "Computer assisted instruction") system, which by the late 1970s supported thousands of terminals globally, introducing many concepts foundational to modern multi-user computing such as forums, instant messaging, and online testing.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-124) In terms of interface technologies, [Donald Bitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Bitzer "Donald Bitzer") was instrumental in the 1960s development of both [touchscreens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen") and [plasma displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_display "Plasma display").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-125) Furthermore, Doug Brown and David R. Woolley created [Talkomatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talkomatic "Talkomatic") in 1973 on the PLATO system, an early online chat system enabling real-time text communication among small groups.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-FalkDrayton-127)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-Bidgoli2004-128)

In the realm of audio-visual technology, [Joseph Tykociński-Tykociner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Tykoci%C5%84ski-Tykociner "Joseph Tykociński-Tykociner") publicly demonstrated for the first time a motion picture with a soundtrack optically recorded directly onto the film in 1922.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-129)

#### Student government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Student government")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg/250px-%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%222010%22_University_of_Illinois.jpg)

[Foellinger Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foellinger_Auditorium "Foellinger Auditorium")

U of I has an extensive history of past student governments. Two years after the university opened in 1868, John Milton Gregory and a group of students created a constitution for a student government. Their governance expanded to the entire university in 1873, having a legislative, executive, and judicial branch. For a period of time, this government had the ability to discipline students. In 1883, however, due to a combination of events from Gregory's resignation to student-faculty infighting, the government formally dissolved itself via [plebiscite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebiscite "Plebiscite").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-149)

It was not until 1934, when the Student Senate, the next university-wide student government, was created. A year before, future Illinois Dean of Students, Fred H. Turner and the university's Senate Committee on Student Affairs gave increased power to the Student Council, an organization primarily known for organizing dances. A year after, the Student Council created a constitution and became the Student Senate, under the oversight of the Committee on Student Affairs. This Student Senate would last for 35 years.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-150) The Student Senate changed its purpose and name in 1969, when it became the Undergraduate Student Association (UGSA). It ceased being a representational government, becoming a [collective bargaining agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining_agency "Collective bargaining agency") instead. It often worked with the Graduate Student Association to work on various projects[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-151)

In 1967, [Bruce A. Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_A._Morrison "Bruce A. Morrison") and other U of I graduate founded the Graduate Student Association (GSA). GSA would last until 1978, when it merged with the UGSA to form the Champaign-Urbana Student Association (CUSA).[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-152)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-illinois1948-153) CUSA lasted for only two years when it was replaced by the Student Government Association (SGA) in 1980. SGA lasted for 15 years until it became the Illinois Student Government (ISG) in 1995. ISG lasted until 2004.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-illinois1948-153)

The current university student government, created in 2004, is the Illinois Student Senate, a combined undergraduate and graduate student senate with 54 voting members. The student senators are elected by college and represent the students in the Urbana-Champaign Senate (which comprises both faculty and students), as well as on a variety of faculty and administrative committees, and are led by an internally elected executive board of a president, external vice president, internal vice president, and treasurer. As of 2012[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit), the executive board is supported by an executive staff consisting of a chief of staff, clerk of the Senate, parliamentarian, director of communications, Intern Coordinator, and the historian of the Senate.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-154)

The university provides housing for undergraduates through [24 residence halls in Urbana and Champaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campus_of_the_University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign#Residence_halls "Campus of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign"). The [Main Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Library_(University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign) "Main Library (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)"), which includes the [Rare Book & Manuscript Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rare_Book_&_Manuscript_Library_(University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign) "The Rare Book & Manuscript Library (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)")

Residence Hall Library System is one of three in the nation.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-162)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-163) The Residence Hall Libraries were created in 1948 to serve the educational, recreational, and cultural information needs of first- and second-year undergraduate students residing in the residence halls, and the living-learning communities within the residence halls. The collection also serves University Housing staff as well as the larger campus community.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-164)[The Rare Book & Manuscript Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rare_Book_&_Manuscript_Library_(University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign) "The Rare Book & Manuscript Library (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)") (RBML) is one of the [Special collections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_collections "Special collections") units within the University Library.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-165) The RBML is one of the largest special collections repositories in the United States.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-166)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-167)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-168)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-169)

The university has several museums, galleries, and archives which include [Krannert Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krannert_Art_Museum "Krannert Art Museum"), [Sousa Archives and Center for American Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sousa_Archives_and_Center_for_American_Music "Sousa Archives and Center for American Music") and [Spurlock Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spurlock_Museum "Spurlock Museum"). Gallery and exhibit locations include [Krannert Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krannert_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "Krannert Center for the Performing Arts") and at [the School of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIUC_College_of_Fine_and_Applied_Arts "UIUC College of Fine and Applied Arts").

The Illinois Open Publishing Network (IOPN) is hosted and coordinated by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Library, offering publishing services to members of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign community, to disseminate [open access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access "Open access")[scholarly publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarly_publication "Scholarly publication").[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-170)

### Recreation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Recreation")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Activities_and_Recreation_Center_%28ARC%29%2C_University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign.jpg/250px-Activities_and_Recreation_Center_%28ARC%29%2C_University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Activities_and_Recreation_Center_(ARC),_University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign.jpg)

[Activities and Recreation Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activities_and_Recreation_Center_(UIUC) "Activities and Recreation Center (UIUC)")

The campus has two main recreation facilities, the [Activities and Recreation Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activities_and_Recreation_Center_(UIUC) "Activities and Recreation Center (UIUC)") (ARC) and the Campus Recreation Center – East (CRCE). Originally known as the Intramural Physical Education Building (IMPE) and opened in 1971, IMPE was renovated in 2006 and reopened in August 2008 as the ARC.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-171) The renovations expanded the facility, adding 103,433 square feet to the existing structure and costing $54.9 million. This facility is touted by the university as "one of the country's largest on-campus recreation centers." CRCE was originally known as the Satellite Recreation Center and was opened in 1989. The facility was renovated in 2005 to expand the space and update equipment, officially reopening in March 2005 as CRCE.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-172)

### Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Transportation")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/CUMTD_Bus_2105.jpg/250px-CUMTD_Bus_2105.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CUMTD_Bus_2105.jpg)

A [Champaign–Urbana Mass Transit District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champaign%E2%80%93Urbana_Mass_Transit_District "Champaign–Urbana Mass Transit District") (MTD) bus

The bus system that operates throughout the campus and community is operated by the [Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champaign-Urbana_Mass_Transit_District "Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District"). The MTD receives a student-approved transportation fee from the university, which provides [unlimited access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_transit_pass "Universal transit pass") for university students, faculty, and staff.

Daily [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") trains through [Illinois Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Terminal "Illinois Terminal") connect Champaign-Urbana with Chicago and [Carbondale, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbondale,_Illinois "Carbondale, Illinois"). This includes the corridor service _[Illini and Saluki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illini\_and\_Saluki "Illini and Saluki")_ and the long-distance _[City of New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City\_of\_New\_Orleans\_(train) "City of New Orleans (train)")_, which provides a direct route to [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"); [Jackson, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi "Jackson, Mississippi"); and [New Orleans, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans,_Louisiana "New Orleans, Louisiana") southbound, in addition to Chicago northbound.

[Willard Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Willard_Airport "University of Illinois Willard Airport"), opened in 1954 and is named for former University of Illinois president Arthur Cutts Willard. The airport is located in Savoy. Willard Airport is home to university research projects, along with flights from [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"). In 2013, the university's [Institute of Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Institute_of_Aviation "University of Illinois Institute of Aviation") was closed at the University of Illinois and the program was transferred to [Parkland College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkland_College_(United_States) "Parkland College (United States)").

### Security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Urbana-Champaign&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Security")]

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has a dedicated police department, UIPD, which operates independently from CPD, the department that serves the surrounding Champaign area.

On June 9, 2017, Yingying Zhang, a Chinese international student, was [abducted and murdered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Yingying_Zhang "Murder of Yingying Zhang") in a case that made national headlines at the time. The university subsequently announced plans to install additional, high-definition, security cameras across the campus.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-WQAD8Security-173)

In July 2022, the university announced that it was partnering with local businesses to invest $300,000 to combat violent crime in Champaign County.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-174)

In September 2022, the City of Champaign transferred responsibility for a large swath of Campustown from CPD (Champaign Police Department) to UIPD, claiming that doing so would reduce response times and improve the quality of service. As part of the jurisdictional reforms, the city agreed to pay a substantial portion of the cost to hire seven new officers to patrol the new coverage area.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-175)

Violent crime fell sharply in 2022 compared to the year prior, with shootings and homicides declining by 50 and 47 percent, respectively. The city attributed the decrease in crime to improved staffing levels and the installation of [automatic license plate readers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_number-plate_recognition "Automatic number-plate recognition").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois#cite_note-176)

The **University of Illinois Chicago School of Law** (**UIC Law**) is the [law school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_school "Law school") of the [University of Illinois Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago "University of Illinois Chicago"), a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois. Founded in 1899, it became affiliated with the university in 2019. The school offers programs for both part-time and full-time students, with both day and night classes available, and offers January enrollment.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

UIC Law was founded in 1899 as the **John Marshall Law School** and initially accredited by the [American Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") in 1951. It merged with the [University of Illinois at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago "University of Illinois at Chicago") in 2019, becoming the University of Illinois Chicago John Marshall Law School.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-4) On May 20, 2021, following review by a university task force, the school announced its official change of name to University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, effective July 1.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-5) The board of trustees acknowledged that "newly discovered research",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6) uncovered by historian [Paul Finkelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Finkelman "Paul Finkelman"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-7) had revealed that influential 19th century [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") chief justice [John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall "John Marshall") was a slave trader and owner who practiced "pro-slavery jurisprudence", which was deemed inappropriate for the school's namesake.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-ChicagoS-T-6)

UIC Law is located in Chicago's central financial and legal district, most commonly known as [The Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). It is across the street from the [Dirksen Federal Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirksen_Federal_Building "Dirksen Federal Building"), which houses the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Seventh_Circuit "U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit") and the [U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._District_Court_for_the_Northern_District_of_Illinois "U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois"), and about four blocks from the [Daley Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daley_Center "Daley Center"), which houses the [Circuit Court of Cook County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_Court_of_Cook_County "Circuit Court of Cook County") and the Bilandic Building site of the [Illinois Appellate Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Appellate_Court "Illinois Appellate Court") (First District). The [Chicago Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bar_Association "Chicago Bar Association") is next door to the law school.

## Admissions and costs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Admissions and costs")]

For the class entering in 2023, UIC Law accepted 69.53% of applicants, with 27.96% of those accepted enrolling. The average enrollee had a 152 [LSAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_School_Admissions_Test "Law School Admissions Test") score and 3.39 undergraduate [GPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grading_in_education#United_States "Grading in education").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-Standard_509-1) Tuition and fees at UIC Law for the 2020-2021 academic year is $39,014 for Illinois residents and $48,014 for out of state residents.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-8)

### Curriculum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Curriculum")]

UIC Law has day and evening divisions, with identical instruction, course content, and scholastic requirements. Lawyering Skills courses, which focus on writing, research, and oral argument, are an integral part of the core curriculum. These courses are taught in small groups, to maximize the individual attention given to each student. A student may earn a J.D. certificate in a certain area of the law or focus more emphatically and earn a joint degree (J.D./LL.M.).

The law school also offers Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Jurisprudence (M.J.) programs for practicing attorneys and non-attorney professionals and other individual students.

UIC School of Law offers seven [Master of Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Laws "Master of Laws") (LL.M.) programs for attorneys seeking specialized education in legal issues and for current J.D. students who would like the maximum concentration in particular areas of the law. UIC Law offers a comprehensive curriculum in the following areas: Employee Benefits Law, Estate Planning, Information Technology and [Privacy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_Law "Privacy Law"), Intellectual Property Law, International Business and Trade Law, [Real Estate Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate"), and Tax Law.

### Journals and organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Journals and organizations")]

There are four honors programs: _UIC Law Review_, _[UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC\_Review\_of\_Intellectual\_Property\_Law "UIC Review of Intellectual Property Law")_ ("RIPL"), the [Moot Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moot_court "Moot court") Honors Program, and the Trial Advocacy & Dispute Resolution Honors Program.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-9) UIC Law sends teams to more than 30 moot court and mock trial competitions annually.

The student community at UIC Law includes more than 50 [student organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_society "Student society") engaging in social awareness, community service, legal discussions, and social activities.

### Clinics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Clinics")]

UIC Law students are required to earn three experiential learning credits – working in a clinic, externship, or a combination of both – in order to graduate. The law school offers students practical opportunities through its seven Community Legal Clinics and more than 50 externship placement sites. Clinics include the Community Enterprise & Solidarity Economy Clinic, Fair Housing Legal Support Center & Clinic, International Human Rights Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Patent Clinic, USPTO-certified IP Trademark Clinic, Pro Bono Litigation Clinic, and the Veterans Legal Clinic. Externship opportunities include judicial, governmental, and non-profit placements, as well as a Semester-in-Practice program that allows JD students to earn a semester of credit hours immersed in a legal market outside of Chicago.

### Global Legal Skills Conference Series

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Global Legal Skills Conference Series")]

The [Global Legal Skills Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Legal_Skills_Conference "Global Legal Skills Conference") Series was founded in 2005 as a forum for professors who teach Legal English and international legal skills to exchange information on teaching techniques and materials.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-10) The conference connects legal writing professionals and other professors who have an interest in teaching international students and lawyers who speak English as a second language.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-11) Since its inception, the Global Legal Skills Conference has been held four times in Chicago, once in Washington, D.C., twice in Mexico, twice in Costa Rica, and twice in Italy.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-12) The conference now also includes presentations of GLS Awards for individual achievement, institutional vision, and outstanding publications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-14)

## Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Library")]

The Louis L. Biro Law Library occupies the 6th – 10th floors of the law school's State Street building. A team of professional librarians and staff members work to serve the students during the 96 hours/week that the library is open. The library holds over 263,003 volumes and microform equivalents and provides on-campus and remote access to some of those titles via their specialty electronic databases. It is continually adding more online subscriptions to its growing collection of electronic resources, including Lexis, Westlaw, [CALI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Computer-Assisted_Legal_Instruction "Center for Computer-Assisted Legal Instruction") Lessons, BNA Premier, IICLE SmartBooks, Max Planck Encyclopedia of Public International Law Online, Justis International Law Reports, Courtroom View Network, which contains audio versions of law school casebooks and streaming trial videos, and Mango languages, an easy to follow system for learning over 20 different languages.

Students have wireless access throughout the law school and the library offers seating for 750, including twelve group study rooms. In addition to supporting the research & instructional needs of the students, faculty & staff of the law school, the library is also open to law school alumni and members of the Chicago Bar Association, whose headquarters building is next door.

## Bar examination passage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bar examination passage")]

In 2023, the overall bar examination passage rate for the law school's first-time examination takers was 59.19%. The average first-time pass rate for [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association") accredited schools was 78.14%. The Ultimate Bar Pass Rate for the school, which the ABA defines as the passage rate for graduates who sat for bar examinations within two years of graduating, was 80.51% for the class of 2021.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-15)

## Employment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Employment")]

According to the school's official [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bar_Association "American Bar Association")-required disclosures for 2023 graduates, within 10 months after graduation 196 (67.59%) of the 290-member graduating class were employed in full-time positions requiring bar passage (i.e. as attorneys) and 17 (5.86%) were employed in full-time JD advantage positions. Attorney positions were in various size law firms, most in 1–10-attorney firms but some in firms exceeding 500 attorneys; 10 graduates obtained local or state judicial clerkships and four obtained federal clerkships. Seventy-five of the class were otherwise employed in public interest, government, higher education, or business. Seventy-two members (24.83%) were unemployed or employed short–term or part–time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_Chicago_School_of_Law#cite_note-16)

[Learn more and register](link_52)

![Image 2: student poses with Thundar during a Discover NDSU event](https://www.ndsu.edu/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_content_promo_default_medium/public/2026-10/2026-04-24-junior-day-discover-230.jpg.webp?itok=Dp5juO70&cb=eacd2302)

## Visit us and discover your moment at NDSU

Visit NDSU in Fargo — big enough to explore, small enough to feel like home. Feel the strength of community and the pride that powers NDSU.

[Visit the campus](link_1)[Meet Fargo](link_29)

![Image 3: students walking past Fargo mural in downtown Fargo](https://www.ndsu.edu/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_content_spotlight_default_medium/public/2025-04/230816_students%20downtown-1168.jpg.webp?itok=HSe5ceQ2&cb=e153c444)

## Bison Today. Bison Forever.

From campus snapshots to alumni milestones, the Herd shows up strong everywhere, every day.

[Explore life at NDSU](link_20)

### It’s going to be a great year!

### Grads helping the next class lead the way

### Alumni shaping a legacy of grit and excellence

## NDSU Impact

As North Dakota’s land-grant, R1 research university, NDSU ranks among the nation’s best in higher education. Students and faculty work together to tackle real challenges, fuel the workforce and shape careers of the future.

### Horizons of new knowledge

Push boundaries in labs, fields and studios with faculty who turn bold ideas into breakthroughs.

[Research at NDSU](link_36)

### **Research in action**

From crop science to cybersecurity, students dive into field-tested, industry-connected work that builds futures and drives progress.

[Industry Relations](link_32)

![Image 4: student weighing samples of dirt on a scale](https://www.ndsu.edu/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_dramatic_side_by_side_default_large/public/2025-05/230214_Natural%20Resources%20Management-72.jpg.webp?itok=-DH6gpqD&cb=d2432222)

## Bison Pride in Motion

[Bison Athletics](link_38)[Move to Mountain West](link_53)

![Image 8: NDSU football team making a big play](https://www.ndsu.edu/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_department_promo_default_images_medium/public/2026-07/20251115-FB-UNI-TS95.jpg.webp?itok=LZr7mgBe&cb=68309b55)![Image 9: NDSU women's soccer team celebrates on the field](https://www.ndsu.edu/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_department_promo_default_images_medium/public/2026-07/NDSU-Soccer-092825-1742-ZL.jpg.webp?itok=EsOM2dYT&cb=2f1d0a8f)

# Submit Data - The Mathematics Genealogy Project

[![Image 1: Tree](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/images/tree-small.gif)](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/index.php)
# Mathematics Genealogy Project

*   [Home](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/index.php)
*   [Search](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/search.php)
*   [Extrema](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/extrema.php)
*   [About MGP](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/about.php)
    *   [Mission](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/mission.php)
    *   [History (PDF)](http://www.ams.org/notices/200708/tx070801002p.pdf)
    *   [Support Us](https://northdakotastate-ndus.nbsstore.net/mathematics-genealogy-project-donation)
    *   [News](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/news.php "Announcements")

    *   [Recognition](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/recognition.php)

*   [Links](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/links.php)
*   [FAQs](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/faq.php "Frequently Asked Questions")
*   [Posters](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/posters.php)
*   [Submit Data](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/submit.php)
*   [Contact](https://www.mathgenealogy.org/contact.php)
*   [Donate](https://northdakotastate-ndus.nbsstore.net/mathematics-genealogy-project-donation)

A service of the [NDSU](https://www.ndsu.edu/)[Department of Mathematics](https://www.ndsu.edu/math/), in association with the [American Mathematical Society](http://www.ams.org/).

# Data Submission

Please enter the name of the mathematician and as much additional information as possible. When you have finished, click on the submit button. Thank you for visiting the Mathematics Genealogy Project web page. We hope you find the information here both interesting and helpful. While you are visiting this site, please keep in mind that this is an ongoing project. Due to the difficulty in obtaining the type of organized data we need, and the varying sources of data, this project is continuously changing.

Not all fields are required to search for a particular mathematician. Partial matches will work as well. See examples and tips below.

First/Given Name
Middle Name
Last/Family Name
Name of School
Year of Degree
Thesis Keyword
Country
Math Subject Class

### Examples

To search for all Mathematicians who received their degree from the University of Wisconsin in 1950:

 Name of School: University of Wisconsin

 Year of Degree: 1950

 To search for anyone whose last name is Jones and their first name begins with a J:

 First Name: J

 Last Name: Jones

### Search Tips

 Recently, Professor George M. Bergman has sent us helpful hints regarding searches: 
1.   If you preface a string with a caret (e.g. ^lee) you will find only those strings that begin with the given string.
2.   Similarly, if you add a dollar sign as a suffix (e.g., lee$) you will find only those strings that end with the given string.
3.   Applying both of the above (e.g., ^lee$) will result in finding only those names that match the string exactly.

Although we now have full support for UTF-8 (Unicode) characters, many of the names in our database appear with unaccented characters due to previous limitations. If you are having trouble finding someone whose name has a non-ASCII character in it, we suggest using an unaccented version of that character in your search ('a' instead of 'ä', for example) or using a substring search that does not include the non-ASCII character. Feel free to submit properly-accented versions of names using the update link on an individual mathematician's page if needed.

# Graph structure

[In July 2016, Cosmin Ionita and Pat Quillen of MathWorks used MATLAB to analyze the Math Genealogy Project graph. At the time, the genealogy graph contained 200,037 vertices. There were 7639 (3.8%) isolated vertices and 1962 components of size two (advisor-advisee pairs where we have no information about the advisor). The largest component of the genealogy graph contained 180,094 vertices, accounting for 90% of all vertices in the graph. The main component has 7323 root vertices (individuals with no advisor) and 137,155 leaves (mathematicians with no students), accounting for 76.2% of the vertices in this component. The next largest component sizes were 81, 50, 47, 34, 34, 33, 31, 31, and 30. For historical comparisonn, we also have data from June 2010, when Professor David Joyner of the United States Naval Academy asked for data from our database to analyze it as a graph. At the time, the genealogy graph had 142,688 vertices. Of these, 7,190 were isolated vertices (5% of the total). The largest component had 121,424 vertices (85% of the total number). The next largest component had 128 vertices. The next largest component sizes were 79, 61, 45, and 42. The most frequent size of a nontrivial component was 2; there were 1937 components of size 2. # Graph structure

[In July 2016, Cosmin Ionita and Pat Quillen of MathWorks used MATLAB to analyze the Math Genealogy Project graph. At the time, the genealogy graph contained 200,037 vertices. There were 7639 (3.8%) isolated vertices and 1962 components of size two (advisor-advisee pairs where we have no information about the advisor). The largest component of the genealogy graph contained 180,094 vertices, accounting for 90% of all vertices in the graph. The main component has 7323 root vertices (individuals with no advisor) and 137,155 leaves (mathematicians with no students), accounting for 76.2% of the vertices in this component. The next largest component sizes were 81, 50, 47, 34, 34, 33, 31, 31, and 30. For historical comparisonn, we also have data from June 2010, when Professor David Joyner of the United States Naval Academy asked for data from our database to analyze it as a graph. At the time, the genealogy graph had 142,688 vertices. Of these, 7,190 were isolated vertices (5% of the total). The largest component had 121,424 vertices (85% of the total number). The next largest component had 128 vertices. The next largest component sizes were 79, 61, 45, and 42. The most frequent size of a nontrivial component was 2; there were 1937 components of size 2. The component with 121,424 vertices had 4,639 root verticies, i.e., mathematicians for whom the advisor is currently unknown. # Top 25 Advisors | Name | Students | | --- | --- | | [C.-C.
